Court of Appeal of Manitoba

R. v. Stevens

Date: 19950222

Docket: ar93-30-01382

ar94-30-01674

SCOTT C.J.M.
(HELPER
J.A. concurring):—The
issue in this case is the constitutional validity of
s. 300
of the
Criminal
Code

which makes it an indictable offence for anyone to "[publish] a
defamatory libel that he knows is false".

There are two appeals before the court. At the
first trial held before L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J., the accused was convicted
of defamatory libel and sentenced to a period of imprisonment of 15 months. He
appeals both conviction and sentence. At the second trial, involving the same
accused but dealing with a different incident, he was acquitted by Simonsen J.
of the Court of Queen's Bench. The Crown appeals.

Certain sections of the
Code,
in addition
to
s. 300
itself, are relevant to these appeals. Section 298 defines
"defamatory libel" as follows:

298(1) A defamatory libel is matter
published, without lawful justifica­tion or excuse, that is likely to injure
the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule,
or that is designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published.

(2) A defamatory libel may be expressed
directly or by insinuation or irony

(a) in words legibly marked upon any
substance; or

(b)
by any
object signifying a defamatory libel otherwise than by words.

Section 299 defines "publishing" as:

299. A person publishes a libel when he

(a) exhibits it in public;

(b) causes it to be read or seen; or

(c)
shows or
delivers it, or causes it to be shown or delivered, with intent that it should
be read or seen by the person whom it defames or by any other person.

The companion section to that in issue in this
appeal is s. 301, which reads as follows:

301. Every one who publishes a defamatory
libel is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term
not exceeding two years.

The essential facts established at the first
trial were that the accused and the complainant had a brief relationship during
the summer of 1991. After the complainant ended the relationship, the accused
displayed a number of posters in the university centre and education buildings
on the University of Manitoba campus. At the time, the complainant was a
student in the Faculty of Education. These posters had a picture of the
complainant and described her, among other things, as being desperate, suicidal
and claimed that she had had an abortion. Shortly after these posters appeared
at the university, the accused placed another poster in the mailbox of two of
the complainant's neighbours. This second poster, which also included the
complainant's picture, described her as a known sex offender.

In a lengthy and carefully reasoned judgment
released on May 21, 1993, and reported at
1993 CanLII 14706 (MB PC)
, 82 C.C.C. (3d) 97, 16 C.R.R. (2d) 91,
[1993] 7 W.W.R. 38, L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J. found that all elements of the
offence under
s. 300
had been proven. She concluded (at pp. 103-4):

Based on the evidence I heard, I found that
the allegations in the posters were false and defamatory, and that Mr. Stevens
intentionally published the posters knowing the contents to be false and
intending to defame the complainant. I was satisfied that Mr. Stevens intended
to injure the complainant's reputation by exposing her to hatred, contempt or
ridicule, and that he intended to insult her Further, I concluded that the
statements in the posters were chosen by Mr. Stevens based on his knowledge of
J.P., that they were malicious and calculated to do the most possible damage to
J.P.'s reputation, and that the places where the posters were published were
selected to maximize their harmful effect on the complainant.

There is no appeal from this finding.

With respect to the constitutionality of s. 300
of the
Code,
L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J. concluded after argument that the
section constituted an infringement of the freedom of expression as guaranteed
by
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
but that it
should none the less be upheld under
s. 1
of the Charter as being a
"reasonable limit prescribed by law" and "demonstrably justified
in a free and democratic society".

R.
v.
Oakes
(1986),

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 24 C.C.C. (3d) 321, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, is the seminal
decision of the Supreme Court which established the criteria that must be met
before it can be said that legislation which otherwise contravenes the
Charter

can none the less be "saved" under
s. 1
. The first criterion relates
to the objective of the legislation which must be of sufficient importance to
justify overriding the protection accorded by the Charter. The second
requirement is that the means chosen to accomplish the objective must meet a
proportionality test. There are three components of this test:

(i) the measures adopted must be carefully
designed to achieve the objective and must be rationally connected to it;

(ii) the means should impair as little as
possible the right or freedom in question; and

(iii) there must be proportionality between
the effects and the objective.

In addressing the objective of the legislation,
L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J. conducted an extensive historical review of the
offence of defamatory libel. She concluded that whereas the purpose of the
offence had in "ancient" times been the prevention of breaches of the
peace, its purpose had now become the protection of reputa­tion which was of
sufficient importance to justify overriding the protection accorded by the

Charter
to freedom of expression.

Dealing with the first component of the
proportionality test, Judge Giesbrecht found that the provision of s. 299(c) of
the
Code,
which defines "publication" as including
communication only to the person defamed, is not rationally connected to the
valid objective of s. 300 since it did not harm reputation. She further
concluded, with respect to the definition of "defamatory libel" in s.
298, that the words "or that is designed to insult the person of or
concerning whom it is published" should be struck down since the inclusion
of "insult" in the definition of "defamatory libel" was
overbroad and did not meet the minimum impairment test. With respect to both,
applying
Schachter
v.
Canada
(1992),
1992 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 93 D.L.R. (4th) 1, [1992] 2
S.C.R. 679, 92 C.L.L.C. ¶14,036, she found that the offending sections could be
severed from ss. 298 and 299 respectively without detracting from the pith and
substance of the legislation, and that Parliament would want the severed
package to remain.

With respect to the final component of the
proportionality test, she held (at p. 153):

Balancing the limited effect of s. 300 on
freedom of expression, against the importance of protection of reputation, I
have little difficulty in concluding that the limitation on the freedom does
not outweigh the importance of the objective.

The accused was, therefore, convicted.

The facts of the second trial held before Simonsen
J. were that the accused mailed a letter to the superintendent of the school
division by whom the same victim was employed alleging that she was mentally
unstable and had allegations of sexual molestation made against her. By an
agreed statement of facts, it was acknowledged that the accusations were false
to the knowledge of the accused. Simonsen J., in his judgment released on March
9, 1994, and reported at
1994 CanLII 16689 (MB QB)
, [1994] 6 W.W.R. 636, 93 Man. R. (2d) 29, 23 W C.B.
(2d) 140, characterized the accused's conduct as follows (at p. 640):
"Accusations of sexual impropriety towards children ... which are known to
be false are, in my view, within the highest order of harm to an individual,
both personally and professionally. The accused's conduct was odious."

With respect to the constitutionality of the
section, Simonsen J. came to the opposite conclusion to that of Giesbrecht Prov.
Ct. J. (By this time the Crown had conceded that the provisions of the sections
in question
prima facie
violated
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
, and the purpose
and object of s. 300 was now an issue.) He was of the opinion that,
historically, intent to defame was not an element of the offence even though
when considering the objectives of Parliament, "[a] strong argument can be
advanced that at the time Parliament adopted the defamatory libel provisions in
1892 there were two objectives in mind, namely, protection of reputation and
also suppression of a breach of the peace" (at pp. 642-3). He further
concluded that the definition of "defamatory libel" failed the
proportionality test in
Oakes

since: "In my view, the provision is
not narrowly targeted to protect the vulnerable against deliberate falsehood
intended to do grave harm to the reputation of an individual. The provision is
too broad in scope to be justified" (at p. 644). He declined to
"excise one portion of the definition of an ingredient of an offence in
order to make it more constitution­ally palatable" (also at p. 644). The
accused was, therefore, acquitted.

History
of
the offence
of
defamatory
libel

The common law

The offence of defamatory libel is of ancient
lineage. As noted in the Supreme Court of Canada decisions in
R.
v.
Keegstra

(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C. (3d) 1 at p. 18, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, 1 C.R. (4th) 129,
and
R. v. Zundel
(1992),
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 75 C.C.C. (3d) 449 at pp. 501-2, 95 D.L.R.
(4th) 202, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 731 (of which more later), the offence of
scandalum
magnatum
(slander of magnates) was first created by the
Statute of
Westminster,
3 Edw. 1, c. 34, in 1275. Not for several centuries thereafter
did the common law courts begin to develop a civil action for slander.
Subsequently, enforcement of the criminal offence became the responsibility of
the infamous Star Chamber and it was not until 1641, following its abolition,
that the Court of King's Bench first acquired jurisdiction with respect to the
offence of criminal libel. At that time, there can be no doubt that the role of
the criminal offence was the preservation of public order, as opposed to the
civil cause of action which was concerned with the protection of private
reputation. As we shall see, problems caused by this historical dichotomy
continue to the present day.

In 1843, as a result of a report of a committee
of the House of Lords, the
Libel Act, 1843 (U.K.),
c. 96
(Lord
Campbell's Act)
was passed. The preamble to
Lord Campbell's Act
described
its purpose as being: "For the better Protection of private Character, and
for more effectually securing the Liberty of the Press, and for better
preventing Abuses in exercising the said Liberty".

It has been accepted ever since that one of the
principal objects of this legislation was to provide a measure of protection to
the press, who frequently appeared as defendants in criminal libel proceedings.
Proceedings for defamatory libel were at times commenced by the Crown at the
urging of prominent persons seeking public vindication, or by way of private
prosecution. Yet, prior to
Lord Campbell's Act,
truth could not be pled
successfully. Truth, while always a defence to a civil action for libel, was
not a defence to a criminal charge of libel since the essence of the offence
continued to be that publication was likely to cause a breach of the peace.
Hence, it was a crime "that the state had an interest in repressing",
the maxim being "the greater the truth, the greater the libel": see
W. Odgers,
An Outline of the Law of Libel
(London: MacMillan
&
Co.
Ltd., 1897), at p. 181. The Act's most significant change, therefore, was to
make truth a defence provided the defendant could prove both that the statement
was true and "that it was for the public benefit that the said matters charged
should be published". This benefit provided a compensat­ing public
advantage to any risk of a breach of the peace. In fact, this change was also
of benefit to the victim. Since evidence of truth was now admissible, the
public would be left in no doubt as to the falseness of the publication should
there be a conviction.

But there was another change as well and that
was the addition of s. 4 to the Act. This section read:

4. And be it enacted, That if any Person
shall maliciously publish any defamatory Libel, knowing the same to be false,
every such Person, being convicted, thereof, shall be liable to be imprisoned
in the Common Gaol or House of Correction for any Term not exceeding Two Years,
and to pay such Fine as the Court shall award.

It is the historical successor of this section,
namely, s. 300 of the present day
Criminal Code
,
that is under scrutiny
in this appeal.

Interestingly, the defence of truth permitted by

Lord Camp­bell's Act
applied to defamatory libel but not to blasphemous
or seditious libel. Thus, if the publication in question concerned a public
person or office and it was alleged that the publication in question was
"calculated and intended to excite hatred of the government and the
administration of the laws, or create dissatis­faction, or disturb the public
peace" (see
R. v. Sullivan (1868), 11
Cox C.C. 44 at p. 51), the
defendant could well be charged with seditious libel. Yet, no evidence as to
the truth of the words could be received.

Although some convictions were obtained in cases
in which a libel was published but where there was little risk of a breach of
the peace being caused in the circumstances, it would seem that this
requirement was still largely accepted as the state of the law of defamatory
libel in England at the time of Confederation: see, for example, Holdsworth,
A
History of the Laws of England, vol.
5;
Fraser on. Libel and Slander,
7th
ed.
(1936),
at p. 210; Folkard,
The Law of Slander and Libel
(London:
Butterworths, 1876), at p. 586; and
R. v. Labouchere
(1884), 12 Q.B.D.
320 at pp. 322-3
,
per
Lord Coleridge C.J.

Typical is the following quotation from Odgers
(at pp. 178 and 181):

Now the State is obviously interested in
repressing all such libels and lampoons as are calculated to provoke a breach
of the peace, or which for any other reason tend to disturb the civil order and
harmony of society. Hence it is a misdemeanour punishable with fine and
imprisonment to write and publish defamatory words of any living person ...
provided ... the publi­cation ... is calculated to cause a breach of the peace.

The State intervenes in the interests of
public peace and order to protect our reputations from wanton and malicious
attacks. It follows, therefore, that not every libel is
a crime, but only those which the State has an interest in repressing.

To complete the historical analysis, in
R.
v.

Wicks
(1936), 25 Cr. App. R. 168, [1936] 1 All E.R. 384
, the court dealt
directly with the issue whether it was an essential ingredient of the offence
to prove that the libel in question was likely to cause a breach of the peace. du
Parcq J. wrote (at pp. 172-3):

It is true that a criminal prosecution for
libel ought not to be instituted, and, if instituted, will probably be regarded
with disfavour by Judge and jury, when the libel complained of is of so trivial
a character as to be unlikely either to disturb the peace of the community or
seriously to affect the reputation of the person defamed. We were referred to
well-known passages in Hawkins' Pleas of the Crown and in the judgment in
LABOUCH) RE
(1884), 12 Q.B.D. 320
, which emphasise this truth, and it may well
be that cases will sometimes occur in which juries may properly refuse to
convict a man accused of criminal libel where the offence is trivial. It is
also true that, as Lush, J., said in HOLBROOK
(1878), 4 Q.B.D. 42, at page 46,
libel is ranked among criminal
offences "because of its supposed tendency to arouse angry passion,
provoke revenge, and thus endanger the public peace." There is, however,
in our judgment, no ground for the suggestion made at the Bar that it is
incumbent upon the prosecution to prove that the libel in question would have
been unusually likely to provoke the wrath of the person defamed, or that the
person defamed was unusually likely to resent an imputation upon his character

In
Gleaves
v.
Deakin,
[1980] A.C.
477, [1979] 2 All
E.R.
497
, the House of Lords decided unanimously that whatever the state
of

the law of defamatory libel may have been with
respect to breach of the peace being an essential element of the offence, it
had by then ceased to be so. But in so concluding, Lord Edmund-Davies made the
following pertinent observations (at p. 490):

It was long considered that criminal
proceedings should not be instituted unless the words were clearly of a kind
calculated to provoke a breach of the peace. If they lacked that essential
quality, judges would direct grand juries to throw out the bill of indictment
and leave the prosecutor to pursue his civil remedies. I need not delay your
Lordships by exploration of this stage in the evolution of criminal libel since
it has already been admirably conducted by Wien J. in
Goldsmith v Pressdram
Ltd.
[1977] Q.B. 83, 90. Suffice it to say that the notion that a tendency
to provoke a breach of the peace is an essential ingredient of the criminal
offence here charged has long been forcefully criticised, as Mr. J. R. Spencer
has demonstrated in his valuable contributions to 1977 Criminal Law Review, at
p. 465, and to
Reshaping the Criminal Law
(1978), p. 266 et seq. Henry
Brougham said 160 years ago that the "allegation of a breach of the peace
was merely a fiction of the law, merely a reason for giving the court
jurisdiction" (1816 Parliamen­tary Debates, vol. 34, ser. 1, p. 387), and
30 years later Lord Campbell said that criminal libel existed simply "with
a view of vindicating the character of the party injured, or of having revenge
upon the libeller, and not in the remotest degree with any view to the protection
of the public peace": House of Lords, Select Committee (1843), vol. 20, p.
177.

(For an excellent discussion on this entire
topic, see the English Law Commission's Working Paper No. 84, "Criminal
Law, Crimi­nal Libel" (London: Her Majesty's Stationery Office, 1982).)

The statutory offence

The genesis of s. 300 lies in an "Act
respecting the Crime of Libel", S.C. 1874, c. 38, which legislation,
including its preamble, essentially mirrored
Lord Campbell's Act.

Section 2 read:

2. Whosoever maliciously publishes any
defamatory libel, knowing the same to be false, is guilty of a misdemeanor ...
.

The above Act was later revised and re-enacted
as an "Act respecting Libel", R.S.C. 1886, c. 163. This provision was
then basically reincorporated in the first Canadian
Criminal Code
enacted
in 1892, and has, in essence, remained the same since that time except for its
transition to an indictable offence. Section 298, the definition section, was
also originally introduced in the 1892
Criminal Code

[c. 29], substantially
in its present form. Undoubt­edly, the requirement that the defamatory libel be
published "without lawful justification or excuse" was intended to
replace the word "maliciously" which was dropped from the then equiva­lent
ss. 300 and 301.

Over the years, a number of Canadian cases have
also adopted the view that a proceeding for criminal libel is not warranted
unless there is some issue as to violation of public rights or a breach of duty
to the community: see, for example,
R.
v.
Cameron
(1898),
1898 CanLII 102 (QC QB)
, 2 C.C.C.
173 (Que. Q.B.);
Menard
v.
The King
(1933),
1933 CanLII 362 (QC KBA)
, 60 C.C.C. 334, [1934]
1 D.L.R. 155, 55 Que. K.B. 90 (App. Div.); and
Maloney v. Fildes
(1932),

1932 CanLII 262 (AB SCTD)
, 60 C.C.C. 7, [1933] 3 D.L.R. 752, [1933] 1 W.W.R. 33 (Alta. S.C.).

The constitutionality
of s.
300

It
is
the position of the accused that not only
s. 300, but the entire defamatory libel part of the
Code,
that is to say
ss. 297 to 316, should be considered since ss. 300 and 301 are, in effect, part
of one and the same offence; the only distinguishing feature between the two
being that with respect to "aggravated libel" (s. 300), the potential
penalty is more severe than with respect to "ordinary libel" (s.
301).

The accused argues that ss. 300 and 301 are part
of a "family" of
Criminal Code

offences which have been
"travelling together" since the time of
Lord Campbell's Act
(1843).
The definition section (s. 298) applies to both ss. 300 and 301 and many of the
defences also apply equally to both (e.g., ss. 305, 307, 308, 309 and 311). I
do not accept the accused's submission. It is s. 300 and the definition
sections alone that are before this court.

Little argument was made respecting s. 301— in
particular, the significance of the fact that it does not require knowledge by
the accused of the falsity.

Dealing with the constitutionality of s. 300, it
is abundantly clear that the section offends the guarantee of freedom of speech
contained in
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
. Freedom of speech occupies a special place
as one of the paramount and important freedoms in our society. As McIntyre J.
noted in
R. W.D.S. U., Local 580
v.
Dolphin Delivery Ltd.
(1986),

1986 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 174 at p. 183, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573, 38 C.C.L.T. 184:

It is one of the fundamental concepts that
has formed the basis for the historical development of the political, social
and educational institutions of western society. Representative democracy, as
we
know it today, which is in great part
the product of free expression and discussion of varying ideas, depends upon
its maintenance and protection.

(See, as well,
Edmonton Journal
v.
Alberta
(Attorney-General)
(1989),
1989 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, 64 D.L.R. (4th) 577, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1326, 41
C.P.C. (2d) 109. Even harmful expression may be protected:
Irwin Toy Ltd.
y.

Quebec (Attorney-General)
(1989),
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, 58 D.L.R. (4th) 577, 25 C.P.R. (3d)
417, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927.)

As McLachlin J. wrote in
Keegstra

(at p.
97):

As this court has repeatedly affirmed, the
content of a statement cannot deprive it of the protection accorded by
s.2
(b),
no matter how offensive it may be. The content of Mr. Keegstra's statements was
offensive and demeaning in the extreme; nevertheless, on the principles
affirmed by this court, that alone would appear not to deprive them of the
protection guaranteed by the
Charter
.

In
Zundel,
McLachlin J., writing for the
majority, made this point with specific reference to false statements (at pp.
510-11):

Before we put a person beyond the pale of
the Constitution, before we deny a person the protection which the most
fundamental law of this land on its face accords to the person, we should, in
my belief, be entirely certain that there can be no justification for offering
protection. The criterion of falsity falls short of this certainty, given that
false statements can sometimes have value and given the difficulty of
conclusively determining total falsity. Applying the broad, purposive
interpretation of the freedom of expression guaranteed by s. 2(b) hitherto
adhered to by this court, I cannot accede to the argument that those who
deliberately publish falsehoods are for that reason alone precluded from
claiming the benefit of the constitutional guarantees of free speech. I would
rather hold that such speech is protected by s. 2(b), leaving arguments
relating to its value in relation to its prejudicial effect to be dealt with
under s. 1.

The content of the communication in question is
irrelevant so long as it conveys or attempts to convey meaning. Only if the
form in which the communication is made itself involves violence or if the
expression takes the form of "direct attack by violent means on the
physical liberty and integrity of another person" (see
Irwin Toy
and

Reference re: ss. 193 and 195.1(1)(c) of the Criminal Code (Man.)
(1990),

1990 CanLII 105 (SCC)
, 56 C.C.C. (3d) 65 at pp. 75-6, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1123, 77 C.R. (3d) 1) will the
communication not receive protection. See also
Canada (Canadian Human Rights
Commission) v. Taylor
(1990),
1990 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, 75 D.L.R. (4th) 577 at p. 591, [1990] 3
S.C.R. 892, 13 C.H.R.R. D/435; and
R. v. Butler
(1992),
1992 CanLII 124 (SCC)
, 70 C.C.C. (3d)
129, 89 D.L.R. (4th) 449, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452. This doubtless explains the
concession made by Crown counsel at the time of the trial before Simonsen J.
and in this court that s. 300 offended
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

Is s. 300 of the Code a "limit
prescribed by law" that is "demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society?"

As noted earlier, the process by which such a
determination should be made by the court has been authoritatively set forth in
the seminal Supreme Court decision of
R.
v.
Oakes
.

At the outset it is important to keep in mind
that the process is not a precise, scientific one. The circumstances of the
particular case are always important since the significance and scope of the
constitutional right that has been restricted, on the one hand, and of the
restriction itself on the other, will vary in each case. As Dickson C.J.C.
warned in
Keegstra
,
"a rigid or formalistic approach to the
application of s. 1 must be avoided". He went on to say (at p. 30):

The ability to use s. 1 as a gauge which is
sensitive to the values and circumstances particular to an appeal has been
identified as vital in past cases ...

the application of the
Oakes

approach
will vary depending on the circumstances of the case, including the nature of
the interests at stake.

Under
Oakes
and the subsequent numerous
cases that have applied it (see, for example,
R. v. Swain
(1991),
1991 CanLII 104 (SCC)
, 63
C.C.C. (3d) 481, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 933, 5 C.R. (4th) 253), the threshold question
is to determine the purpose and object of the legislation. Only if this is of
sufficient importance to warrant overriding the constitutionally protected
right of freedom need the court then pass on to consideration of the
proportionality test, to ascertain if the means chosen to achieve that
objective are proportional. To be of sufficient importance, the objective must
be "pressing and sub­stantial in a free and democratic society".

Can there be a shifting purpose?

In this instance we are dealing with a statute
that has remained the same in substance for over 100 years. It is over 150
years since the enactment of
Lord Campbell's Act.
One of the first
questions to be dealt with, therefore, relates to the relevant time-period to
consider the purpose and object of the legislation. Should the court answer
this question having regard only to the circumstances that existed in 1892, or
can the court ascribe or "read in" to the legislation a purpose and
object consistent with modern cir­cumstances and views?

The answer to this question is all the more
important given the strong submission made by the Crown that this court, if
given the choice between a purpose and object that is consistent with modern

Charter
principles and one that is not, can simply choose the former. See the
comment of Gonthier J. in
R.
v.
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
(1992),

1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, 74 C.C.C. (3d) 289 at p. 326, 93 D.L.R. (4th) 36, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 606:

It must be remembered that if there are two
possible interpretations of a statutory provision, one of which embodies the

Charter
values and the other does not, that which embodies the Charter values
should be adopted: see
Hills v. Canada (Attorney-General)
(1988),
1988 CanLII 67 (SCC)
,
48
D.L.R.
(4th) 193, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 513, 88 C.L.L.C. ¶14,011.

The Supreme Court first dealt with the question
whether there could be a "shifting purpose" (for
Charter
purposes) in

R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, 18 D.L.R. (4th)
321, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, and rejected such concept despite its undoubted
acceptance in the United States. Dickson J. (as he then was), writing for five
of a six-judge panel, wrote (at p. 417):

... the theory of a shifting purpose stands
in stark contrast to fundamental notions developed in our law concerning the
nature of "Parliamentary intention". Purpose is a function of the
intent of those who drafted and enacted the legislation at the time, and not of
any shifting variable.

The Supreme Court has reaffirmed its rejection
of the shifting purposes approach in numerous subsequent decisions. While
modern reality and circumstances may, as always, justify a court in
reinterpreting the scope of the legislation in question so as to change its
emphasis, the court cannot reinvent or change alto­gether the fundamental
objective of the legislation. This is made plain by the following passage from
Zundel

(at p. 513):

In determining the objective of a
legislative measure for the purposes of s. 1, the court must look at the
intention of Parliament when the section was enacted or amended. It cannot
assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived current
utility of the impugned provision: see
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 18 C.C.C.
(3d) 385 at pp. 415-6, 18 D.U.R. (4th) 321 at pp. 351-2, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, in which this court
rejected the U.S. doctrine of shifting purposes. Although the application and
interpreta­tion of objectives may vary over time (see, e,g.,
Butler, supra,
per Sopinka J., at pp.
157-9 C.C.C., pp. 477-9 D.L.R.), new and altogether different purposes should
not be invented. ... To convert s. 181 into a provision directed at encouraging
racial harmony is to go beyond any permissible shift in emphasis and effectively
rewrite the section.

While a "shift in emphasis" can take
place — for example, the extent to which a purpose or object remains or becomes
pressing and substantial can change over time (see
Irwin
Toy) — there
cannot be a wholesale change in the objectives of the legislation.

What are the purposes and objectives of the
legislation?

At the conclusion of argument some months ago,
it was my impression that s. 300 of the
Code
could not pass the
threshold test. From an examination of the authorities and of the references
earlier noted (they are but a representative sample), it seemed reasonably
certain that breach of the peace was at least the principal objective of
Lord
Campbell's Act.
Such an objective in 1994 or 1995 can hardly be said to be
pressing and substantial.

This point of view was reinforced by the fact
that the efficacy of the offence had lately come under criticism. In Canada,
perhaps even more so than in England, the offence has fallen into a virtual
state of disuse. The Law Reform Commission of Canada in its Working Paper No.
35, "Defamatory Libel", 1984, described prosecutions for the offence
in Canada as "rare" and noted that in the 10-year period between 1963
and 1973, there were only 36 prosecutions (excluding Quebec) and only one in each
of the years 1972 and 1973.

J. R. Spencer in his article, "Criminal
Libel — A Skeleton in the Cupboard", [1977] Grim. L.R. 383 at p. 389,
noted that while trials for criminal libel in England appeared to be fairly
frequent at the turn of the century, even up to the beginning of World War II,
the numbers fell sharply thereafter to the point where it had fallen into
general disuse by the 1970s. Professor Ian Loveland in his article,
"Defamation of `government': taking lessons from Amer­ica?" (Butterworths,
Legal Studies, The Journal of the Society of Public Teachers of Law, vol. 14,
No. 2, November, 1994), writes (at p. 218): "... it would seem plausible
to conclude that in Britain, prosecution for libellous speech has shed its
legitimacy as a result of prolonged disuse".

In
Zundel,
a case relied on very heavily
by counsel for Stevens, the Supreme Court struck down s. 181 of the
Code,
which
made it an offence to wilfully publish a false statement that the person knew
to be false and that is likely to cause injury or mischief to a public
interest,
inter alia,
because it failed to pass the threshold test under
s. 1. In so concluding, McLachlin J. noted that the section had been rarely
used despite its long history, and that "[1]ies for the most part, have
historically been left to the civil law of libel and slander" (at p. 522).
In the circumstances, therefore, she questioned whether it was necessary to
invoke "the rigorous sanction of criminal conviction and
imprisonment" (at p. 510). Indeed, she herself arguably hinted at a
similar fate for the offence of defamatory libel when she noted with respect to
this offence (as well as the offences of blasphemy and sedition) that they
"appear to be rarely if ever used and the constitutionality of which may
be open to question".

But I have since concluded that s. 300 responds
to a matter of pressing and substantial concern in today's society even though
it has essentially remained unchanged since
Lord Campbell's Act.
I say
this for two reasons. Firstly, because I am now convinced that protection of
reputation was and continues to be, along with protection of the press, the
significant objective of the legislation and, secondly, because the majority of
the commentary earlier referred to respecting the offence of defamatory libel
while perhaps applicable to what is now s. 301 of the
Code,
did not
advert to the much stricter offence of "knowing" or
"aggravated" defamatory libel encompassed by what is now s. 300.

That protection of reputation was at least one
of the principal aims of
Lord Campbell's Act
cannot be doubted. My
colleague Twaddle J.A. has impressively analyzed its legislative history in his
extensive reasons and, therefore, this task need not be duplicated here. I
repeat but one reference, namely, that contained in a revised version of Thomas
Starkie's
The Law of Slander and Libel,
6th ed. (London: William Clowes
& Sons Ltd., 1897), edited by Henry Folkard, where in the footnote the
author noted:

The true principle would seem to be, that a
libel on a private individual should be punished as a criminal offence for the
protection of
individual character, or for reputation's sake,
as
well
as for the preservation of public peace;
both the private individual and
the public would then be protected, upon the same principles as in the cases of
assault and battery.

(Emphasis in original.)

Although such legislative history is undoubtedly
now admissi­ble, especially in
Charter
cases, to assist in determining the
purpose for which the legislation was enacted, it is ordinarily given minimal
weight: see
Reference re: Section 94(2) of the Motor Vehicle Act
(1985),

1985 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, 23 C.C.C. (3d) 289, 24 D.L.R. (4th) 536, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 486, where Lamer J.
(as he then was) noted that minutes of proceedings of parliamentary committees
and the like, "though admissible, and granted somewhat more weight than
speeches, should not be given too much weight" (at p. 306). Legislative
intent is still derived primarily from the legislation itself: see
Hunter v.
Southam Inc.
(1984),
1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, 14 C.C.C. (3d) 97, 11 D.L.R. (4th) 641, [1984] 2
S.C.R. 145, which, of course, includes the preamble. But in this case, the
parliamentary history is especially pertinent, given the pre-eminence of the
members of the special committee. It is quite clear, on reviewing the numerous
references to the objectives of
Lord Campbell's Act
earlier referred to,
that no one, except Professor Starkie (and thereafter the new editor Folkard),
adverted to the new emphasis on protection of reputation. It was left to the
courts in the 90-odd years that followed, between
Lord Campbell's Act
and

Wicks, supra,
to eventually confirm this new reality.

Equally surprising is the lack of attention paid
to the new offence under s. 4 of
Lord Campbell's Act,
of knowing or
aggra­vated defamatory libel. While I cannot agree (as Twaddle J.A.'s judgment
seems to suggest) that protection of reputation was the sole purpose of this
new offence, by virtue of the very nature of the offence, it must none the less
be a paramount objective. Perhaps the explanation, for what may seem to us now
to be such a glaring oversight, is simply that the purpose and object of the
legislation in 1843, or for that matter in 1892, was of no practical
importance. It was only when the
Canadian Charter
was intro­duced in 1982 that
it became of significance in this country for a
s. 1
analysis. Indeed, this is
the first case in Canada in which such a task has had to be undertaken.

In my opinion, the ancient tenet that the
impugned libel constituted an offence because of its supposed tendency to
endanger the public peace has, consequent upon the enactment of
Lord
Campbell's Act,
gradually disappeared. It has been replaced by the
requirement that there be some public component or interest in the proceedings.
Simply put, if this were not so, it would not be the business of the criminal
law to intervene. If there was any doubt about this following the decision in
Wicks,

it was removed when the House of Lords decided
Gleaves v. Deakin,
in
1979. Lord Diplock noted (at p. 483):

My Lords, public authority, represented in
criminal matters by the Director of Public Prosecutions and the police, has had
minimal recourse in recent years to prosecutions for the offence of defamatory
libel; and I have no reason to doubt that in each of the prosecutions which its
representatives have brought it could be shown not only that the defamatory
matter was false but also that by reason of its nature or the circumstances in
which it was published, repression of the publication
by penal sanctions was necessary in the public interest.

Lord Scarman put it even more succinctly (at pp.
494-5):

It is, however, not every libel that
warrants a criminal prosecution. To warrant prosecution the libel must be
sufficiently serious to require the intervention of the Crown in the public
interest.

... it is the gravity of the libel which
matters. The libel must be more than of a trivial character: it must be such as
to provoke anger or cause resentment. In my judgment, the references in the
case law to reputation, outrage, cruelty or tendency to disturb the peace are
no more than illustrations of the various factors which either alone or in
combination contribute to the gravity of the libel. The essential feature of a
criminal libel remains — as in
the past—the publication of a grave, not trivial, libel.

Exactly how far this change in objective — from
preventing a breach of the peace to encompassing matters which the state has an
interest in repressing —had progressed by 1892 when Canada's first
Criminal
Code

was enacted is not clear and can only be guessed at. What is clear,
however, is that the change was well under way and that protection of character
or reputation was by then a significant goal of what is now s. 300.

In my opinion, s. 300 more than satisfies the
threshold require­ment of a s. 1 analysis.

Proportionality

The first subcomponent of the proportionality
test is that the means chosen to achieve the objective must be "rationally
connected" to it and not be arbitrary, unfair or based on irrational
considerations.

In
Zundel,
the majority simply assumed
such a rational link and moved directly to consider the second criterion of the
propor­tionality test, namely, minimal impairment. Here, there is an obvious
rational connection between the purpose and object of s. 300 as just
identified, and the offence of aggravated defamatory libel. Nothing more need
be
said
of it.

Before this court, much argument was addressed
to the issue of the
mens rea
requirement of the offence. The Crown's
argument is that intention to publish and intention to deliberately and falsely
defame are both an essential element of the offence. Hence, the offence is not
only rationally linked to the primary social objective of the legislation,
namely, protection of reputation, but results in minimal impairment. At least,
the Crown argues, the matter is so ambiguous as to enable this court to infer a
"high
mens rea
requirement" for the offence: see
Beaver
y.

The Queen
(1957),
1957 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 118 C.C.C. 129, [1957] S.C.R. 531, 26 C.R. 193, and
R.

v.
Sault Ste. Marie (City)
(1978),
1978 CanLII 11 (SCC)
, 40 C.C.C. (2d) 353, 85 D.L.R.
(3d) 161, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1299.

Next to the issue of the purpose and object of
s. 300, this is undoubtedly the most contentious issue before this court.

The importance of determining whether specific
mens
rea
to defame is required is, of course, not an academic exercise. In
Keegstra
,

a very important factor in the court's conclusion that the provision of the

Code
prohibiting wilful promotion of hatred against identifiable groups
did not offend the minimal impairment test was because "the provision
possesses a stringent
mens rea
requirement, necessitating either an
intent to promote hatred or knowledge of the substantial certainty of such
..." (at p. 66). This is to be contrasted with
Zundel
where,
"[t]he
mens rea
lies in the knowledge that the statement is
false" (at p. 503), an especially difficult hurdle when dealing with
historical facts.

The Crown essentially conceded that to pass the
minimal impairment test, intention to defame must be an element of the offence
with the burden of proof being borne by the Crown. If this criterion is met,
the requirement of minimal impairment has demonstrably been achieved since a
prosecution can then only succeed when, by definition, the accused was guilty
of the serious crime of character assassination.

Before embarking on an examination of the law,
it is essential to recall that the requirement of minimal impairment does not
mandate a standard of perfection. It is not only the least intrusive
legislative enactment that will pass constitutional muster: see
Keegstra
,
per
Dickson C.J.C., at pp. 64-5.

Incredibly, the law respecting the requirement
by the Crown to prove an intention to defame is even less clear than that just
canvassed regarding the purpose and object of the legislation.

Counsel for Stevens strongly asserted that
precedent combined with the wording of s. 298 — which defines "defamatory
libel" as a matter published "that is likely to injure the reputation
of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or that is designed
to insult" — can only lead to one conclusion, namely, that the Crown need
only prove intention to publish.

There is considerable authority to support this
assertion. A typical turn-of-the-century textbook reference asserting that
proof of intention to defame is not an element of defamatory libel is W. Odgers,

Libel and Slander
(London: MacMillan & Co. Ltd., 1881), at p. 388.
R.

v.
Munslow,
[1895] 1 Q.B. 758
, is often cited as authority for the
proposition that intention to defame is not an element in the offence of defamatory
libel. In particular, much emphasis is placed on the statement made by Lord
Russell of Killowen C.J. (at p. 761): "... the law attaches to the fact of
publication the inference that the publication was malicious". But the
context in which those words were written casts doubt on whether the court
intended to make a sweeping statement about criminal intent, since the issue
before the court was the meaning of the word "maliciously" used in
both ss. 4 and 5 of
Lord Campbell's Act.
The court simply considered
that malice was synonymous with a lack of legal excuse of justification.

In
R.
v.
Lemon,
[1979] A.C. 617,
[1979] 1 All E.R. 898
, the House of Lords, by a narrow majority, concluded that
intention to publish was sufficient to secure a conviction for the offence of
publishing a blasphemous libel. While, like my colleague Twaddle J.A., I much
prefer the reasoning of the minority (Lords Diplock and Edmund-Davies), I note
in any event that the case deals only with blasphemous libel. In
The Liberty
of the Press, Speech and Public Worship
(London: MacMillan & Co. Ltd.,
1880),
J.
Paterson, in comparing seditious and blasphemous libels on the
one hand, with defamatory libels on the other, writes (at p. 142):

The difference between these and a
defamatory libel or a libel on individuals is so great, that they can scarcely
be classed together, and the characteristics of the one cannot be compared with
those of the other, except that they both in some way qualify the primary right
of free speech.

In addition, counsel for Stevens cites the
obiter

comments of this court in
R.
v.
Law
(1909),
1909 CanLII 302 (MB CA)
, 19 Man. R. 259,
as well as the decision in
R.
v.
Georgia Straight Publishing Ltd.,
McLeod and Cummings,
1969 CanLII 834 (BC SC)
, [1970] 1 C.C.C. 94, 4 D.L.R. (3d) 383, 6 C.R.N.S. 150
(B.C. Co. Ct.).

In
Wicks,
the Court of Criminal Appeal in
dealing with a charge of aggravated defamatory libel said (at p. 174):

There is no doubt that, under such a count,
it is for the prosecution to satisfy the jury that the defendant had such
knowledge, and that the burden of proving that he had not such knowledge never
lies upon the defendant. In the present case, we see no reason for holding that
the prosecution did not fully discharge the burden which rested upon them.
The
falsity of the libel is to be presumed, and, in the absence of a plea of
justification, could not be questioned.

(Emphasis added.)

No less an authority than Halsbury's Laws of
England in both its third and fourth editions relies on this case as authority
for the proposition that in the absence of a plea of justification the
defamatory statement must be assumed to be false. As my colleague Twaddle J.A.
has pointed out, this interpretation ignores the contrary decision of the same
court four years earlier in
R.
v.
Black,
The Times, November 16,
1932. But proving knowledge of

on a reasonable interpretation of its
history and on the plain reading of its text, is subject to two equally persuasive interpretations, the court should
adopt that interpretation which accords with the
Charter
and the values to
which it gives expression
(Hills
and
Slaight, supra).

Mens rea
may
consist either of intention to do the immediate act or to bring about the
consequence of that act, depending on the circumstances. In
R. v. Théroux
(1993),

1993 CanLII 134 (SCC)
, 79 C.C.C. (3d) 449, 100 D.L.R. (4th) 624, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 5, the Supreme Court
considered the elements of the offence of fraud. McLachlin J. in discussing the
element of
mens rea
noted (at p. 458):

Mens rea,
on the other hand, refers to the guilty
mind, the wrongful intention, of the accused. Its function in criminal law is
to prevent the conviction of the morally innocent — those who do not understand
or intend the consequences of their acts. Typically,
mens rea
is
concerned with the consequences of the prohibited
actus reus.

Although
Théroux
was not a
Charter
case,
the decision clearly reflects Charter principles. It is entirely proper for a
court to define an offence in such a way that it includes within its elements
only what can truly be said to be criminal conduct.

Thus it is that the historical context of the
offence, including the development of a public element as a purpose and object
of the offence, together with the modern-day constitutional demands as mandated
by the
Charter
all point in the same direction, namely, that the Crown must prove
an intention to defame on the part of an accused in order to successfully
prosecute proceedings for defamatory libel.

This conclusion effectively disposes of the
appeal. It automati­cally follows that the offence thus narrowly confined in
its objectives and elements can only apply to the most egregious and deliberate
of character assassination. As such, it minimally impairs freedom of
expression. I agree with the comments of Twaddle J.A. with respect to the other
elements of proportionality. It is not necessary for me to go into the other
issues.

The appeal from the conviction obtained before
L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J. is, therefore, dismissed; the appeal from the
acquittal by Simonsen J. is, accordingly, allowed and a conviction entered.
Sentencing will have to proceed before Simonsen J.

and

Freedom of speech and freedom of expression were
well-known and accepted concepts long before the

v.
Canada (Public Service Staff Relations Board)

...
it is equally obvious that free
speech or expression is not an absolute, unqualified value.
Other values
must be weighed with it. Sometimes these other values supplement, and build on,
the value of speech. But in other situations there is a collision. When that
happens the value of speech may be cut back if the competing value is a
powerful one. Thus, for example, we have laws dealing with libel and slander,
sedition and blasphemy. We also have laws imposing restrictions on the press in
the interests of, for example, ensuring a fair trial or protecting the privacy
of minors or victims of sexual assaults.

A similar type of balancing is required in
the present appeal. Public servants have some freedom to criticize the
government. But it is not an absolute freedom.

(Emphasis added.)

of the historical develop­ment of the political, social and educational
institutions of western society. Representative democracy, as we know it today,
which is in great part the product of free expression and discussion of varying
ideas, depends upon its maintenance and protection.

Yet three short years after the decision in
Dolphin
Delivery,
Dickson C.J.C. suggested that freedom of expression extended to
almost any activity which has a meaning. And he noted in his reasons for
decision in
Irwin Toy Ltd.
v.
Quebec (Attorney-General)

(1989),

1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, 58 D.L.R. (4th) 577 at p. 607, 25 C.P.R. (3d) 417, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927:
"... if the activity conveys or attempts to convey a meaning, it has
expressive content and
prima facie
falls within the scope of the
guarantee."

And in
R.
v.
Keegstra
,
McLachlin
J. re-emphasizes the breadth of
s. 2
(b) in these terms (at p. 97): "...
the content of a statement cannot deprive it of the protection accorded by
s.
2
(b) [of the
Charter
], no matter how offensive it may be."

One cannot ignore the wide reach of freedom of
expression as manifested in these quotations. At the same time, no jurist has
proclaimed that the freedom is absolute. Judges of the Supreme Court have
continued to relate freedom of expression with the flowering of democracy and
the interchange of ideas which are indispensable to a healthy society.

Thus, in the
Keegstra

case, Dickson
C.J.C., writing for the majority, expanded upon the fundamental role of freedom
of expression in our democratic process. He wrote (at p. 48):

At the core of freedom of expression lies
the need to ensure that truth and the common good are attained, whether in
scientific and artistic endeavours or in the process of determining the best
course to take in our political affairs.

He went on to comment (at pp. 49-50):

The connection between freedom of
expression and the political process is perhaps the linchpin of the s. 2(b)
guarantee, and the nature of this connection is largely derived from the
Canadian commitment to democracy. Freedom of expression is a crucial aspect of
the democratic commitment, not merely because it permits the best policies to
be chosen from among a wide array of proffered options, but additionally
because it helps to ensure that participation in the political process is open
to all persons. Such open participation must involve to
a substantial degree the notion that all persons are equally deserving of
respect and dignity. The state therefore cannot act to hinder or condemn a
political view without to some extent harming the openness of Canadian
democracy and its associated tenet of equality for all.

In its earlier
per curiam
judgment in
Ford
v. Quebec (Attorney-General)
(1988),
1988 CanLII 19 (SCC)
, 54 D.L.R. (4th) 577 at p. 617, [1988]
2 S.C.R. 712, 10 C.H.R.R. D/5559, the court adopted the values justifying the
constitutional protection of freedom of expression that were summarized by
Professor Thomas I. Emerson in his article, Toward a General Theory of the
First Amendment" (1963), 72 Cale L.J. 877 at p. 878:

The values sought by society in protecting
the right to freedom of expression may be grouped into four broad categories.
Maintenance of a system of free expression is necessary (1) as assuring
individual self-fulfillment, (2) as a means of attaining the truth, (3) as a
method of securing participation by the members of the society in social,
including political, decision-making, and (4) as maintaining the balance
between stability and change in society.

The court also approved the three
"rationales" referred to by professor Robert J. Sharpe in his
article, "Commercial Expression and the
Charter
" (1987), 37 U.T.L.J.
229 at p. 232:

The first is that freedom of expression is
essential to intelligent and democratic self-government ... . The second theory
is that freedom of expression protects an open exchange of views, thereby
creating a competi­tive market-place of ideas which will enhance the search for
the truth ... . The third theory values expression for its own sake. On this
view, expression is seen as an aspect of individual autonomy. Expression is to
be protected because it is essential to personal growth and self-realization.

The court then went on to explain that those
values raise two questions, and two separate analytical processes, under the
Charter
.
The court wrote (at pp. 617-8):

While these attempts to identify and define
the values which justify the constitutional protection of freedom of expression
are helpful in emphasizing the most important of them, they tend to be
formulated in a philosophical context which fuses the separate questions of
whether a particular form or act of expression is within the ambit of the
interests protected by the value of freedom of expression and the question
whether that form or act of expression, in the final analysis, deserves
protection from interference under the structure of the
Canadian Charter
and
the Quebec Charter. These are two distinct questions and call for two distinct
analytical processes. The first, at least for the Canadian Charter, is to be
determined by the purposive approach to interpretation set out by this court in
Hunter v.
Southam Inc.

(1984),
1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, 11 D.L.R. (4th) 641, 14 C.C.C. (3d) 97,
[1984] 2 S.C.R. 145, and
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
[(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 18 D.L.R. (4th)
321, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295]. The second, the question of the
limitation on the protected values, is to be determined under
s. 1
of the
Charter as interpreted in
Oakes

(1986),
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200, 24 C.C.C.
(3d) 321, [[1986] 1 S.C.R. 103], and
R. v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd.
(1986),

1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 35 D.L.R. (4th) 1, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 385, [1986] 2 S.C.R.
713. The division between the two analytical processes has been established by
this court in the above decisions. First, consideration will be given to the
interests and purposes that are meant to be protected by the particular right
or freedom in order to determine whether the right or freedom has been
infringed in the context presented to the court. If the particular right or
freedom is found to have been infringed, the second step is to determine
whether the infringement can be justified by the state within the constraints
of s. 1. It is within the perimeters of s. 1 that courts will in most instances
weigh competing values in order to determine which should prevail.

It is the first question— whether the activity
of the accused "is within the ambit of the interests protected by the
value of freedom of expression" — and the consideration that is to be
given to "the interests and purposes that are meant to be protected"
by freedom of expression, that, in our view, are at the heart of this case.

It was in
Irwin Toy Ltd.

(which was
argued before the Supreme Court at the same time as
Ford v. Quebec)
that
the court pronounced the virtually unlimited reach of
s. 2
(b). Like
Ford
v.

Quebec, Irwin Toy
was a commercial expression case. It involved a
provision in the Quebec
Consumer Protection Act
which prohib­ited
television advertising directed at persons under 13 years of age. It was not
the stuff out of which one would expect the court to formulate a sweeping and
comprehensive approach to the assess­ment of an individual's
s. 2
(b) rights.
But as we see in the court's later decisions
(Reference re:
ss. 193
and
195.1(1)(c) of the Criminal Code (Man.)
(1990),
1990 CanLII 105 (SCC)
, 56
C.C.C. (3d) 65, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1123, 77 C.R. (3d) 1;
R. v. Keegstra
, supra;
R.
v.
Butler
(1992),
1992 CanLII 124 (SCC)
, 70 C.C.C. (3d) 129, 89 D.L.R. (4th) 449, [1992]
1 S.C.R. 452; and
R.
v.
Zundel
(1992),
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 75 C.C.C. (3d) 449, 95
D.L.R. (4th) 202, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 731; are examples), that has been the result.

The first step in the analysis of a freedom of
expression challenge is set out in the judgment of the majority in
Irwin Toy

(delivered by Dickson C.J.C., Lamer and Wilson JJ.) at p. 606. It is,

... to discover whether the activity which
the plaintiff wishes to pursue may properly be characterized as falling within
"freedom of expression". If the activity is not within
s. 2
(b), the
government action obviously cannot be challenged under that section.

However, the Chief Justice
et al.
go on
to state (at p. 607):

We cannot, then, exclude human activity
from the scope of guaranteed free expression on the basis of the content or
meaning being conveyed. Indeed, if the activity conveys or attempts to convey a
meaning, it has expressive content and prima
facie
falls within the
scope of the guarantee.

In the
Irwin Toy
case and in subsequent
decisions, the Supreme Court has suggested that there is virtually no
limitation on freedom of expression with respect to content, but that there can
be limitations with respect to the form of expression. Thus (using the same
example as Lamer C.J.C. in his reasons in
Committee for the Commonwealth of
Canada
v.
Canada
(1991),
1991 CanLII 119 (SCC)
, 77 D.L.R. (4th) 385 at pp. 395-6, [1991] 1
S.C.R. 139, 4 C.R.R. (2d) 60), picketing on a busy highway may fall outside

Charter
protection because of the form rather than the content of the
expression. Shouting obsceni­ties on the street corner deserves
s. 2
(b)
protection, but not if the shouting occurs in the quiet room of a public
library.

The form it takes may indeed disentitle
expression to
s. 2(b)

Charter
protection, but if strange anomalies are to be
avoided the limitations on the freedom must extend to content as well.
Otherwise, using
R.
v.
Clemente
as an example, the threat to kill
is expression falling within
s. 2
(b) if made in the office of the complainant's
supervisor, but probably not if shouted out in a public library.

There still should be room to conclude that the
message itself is not deserving of
Charter
protection in whatever form it may
come.

Our colleague, Twaddle J.A., warns that if
judges are left to determine what words are deserving of
Charter
protection and
what words are not, what words serve one of the underlying values and what
words do not, instead of the fear of tyranny by government
we
will have
substituted fear of tyranny by judges. One might observe, however, that the
content of the message is often the crucial factor in deciding whether speech
is entitled to constitutional protection in the United States. Indeed, it would
be a virtual certainty that the kind of expression by the accused in the
present case would not be accorded constitutional protection in any of the
states of the union. Yet the weighing of the worth of the content has not led to
a tyranny of judges
in
the United States. If s. 1 becomes the sole mechanism for denying
expression constitutional protection on the basis of content, then another
danger arises, namely, that the application of s. 1 will become distorted in
favour of government. If that occurs, a limitation of Charter rights of every
kind will be the unfortunate result.

In his article, "The Supreme Court's
Approach to Freedom of Expression — Irwin Toy v. Quebec (Attorney-General) —
And the Illusion of Section 2(b) Liberalism" (1993), 3 N.J.C.L. 37, M.
David Lepofsky writes persuasively that in
Irwin
Toy the Supreme Court
went far beyond what was necessary to decide the issue that was before it; and
that the comprehensive test the court enunciated for the determination of free
expression challenges was fundamentally flawed. The author also expresses the
view that the court's "broad, sweeping construction of the freedom of
expression ... will undoubtedly send a great number of cases on to a s. 1 'reasonable
limits' analysis ... [and] in turn place enormous pressure on courts to greatly
diminish the s. 1 standard which government must meet". He concludes (at
p. 93):

It is far preferable to place some more
meaningful constraints on
section 2
(b)'s scope in order to skim out the non-compelling
cases at the
section 2
(b) stage. Thereafter claims which pass the section 2(b)
stage would be subjected to a strict section 1 standard. This will yield
greater judicial consistency and predictability. It will provide more effective
protection for
section 2
(b) values in the long run.

Professor Peter W. Hogg expresses a similar
concern in his text,
Constitutional Law of Canada,
3rd ed. (Toronto: Carswell,
1992) (loose-leaf, vol. 2, at para. 40.5(d), p. 40-12):

The principle of content neutrality means
that s. 2(b) extends to much activity that is not worthy of constitutional
protection. Indeed, the Court has acknowledged that "not all expression is
equally worthy of protection". The evaluation of the worthiness of the
expression is however relevant only to the s. 1 inquiry. If the Court regards a
particular kind of expression as of little value, then this makes the objective
of a limiting law easier to justify, and invites more relaxed standards of
proportionality. Because communicat­ing for the purpose of prostitution, or
promoting racial hatred, are of "limited importance", it is
relatively easy to justify laws that prohibit those activities. This
illustrates my earlier point that the expansion of the guaranteed right, in
this case
s. 2
(b), inevitably leads to an erosion of the severe standards of
justification that the Court originally erected for s. 1. That in turn leads to
decisions that depend heavily on the judges' balancing of costs and benefits, a
process that is unprincipled and unpredictable.

In an earlier article, "Interpreting the

Charter of Rights
: Generosity and Justification" (1990), 28, Osgoode Hall
L.J. 817 at p. 819, Professor Hogg explains why a "generous"
interpretation of rights is incompatible with a stringent standard of justification
under s. 1:

The Court's decision in
Oakes

to
prescribe a single standard of justification for all rights, to make that
standard a high one, and to cast the burden of satisfying it on the government
entails a corresponding caution in defining the guaranteed rights. Each right
should be so interpreted as not to reach behaviour that is outside the purpose
of the right—behaviour that is not worthy of constitutional protection. If this
is ignored, the inevitable result will be the erosion of the
Oakes

standard
of justification; it can be taken for granted that the Court will find a way of
upholding legislation in the face of
Charter

claims that are regarded by
the judges as weak.

The reason that generosity should give way,
rather than the stringent standard of justification, concerns the policy-making
role of the courts. If the scope of the guaranteed rights is wide, and the
standard of justification is relaxed, then a large number of
Charter

challenges
will come before the courts and will fall to be determined
under section 1. Since section 1 requires that the policy of the legislation be
balanced against the policy of the
Charter,
and since it is difficult to devise meaningful standards to
constrain the balancing process, judicial review will become even more
pervasive, even more policy-laden, and even more unpredictable than it is now.

Mr. Lepofsky comes to precisely the same
conclusion as Profes­sor Hogg. In a second article, "Making Sense of the
Libel Chill Debate: Do Libel Laws "Chill" the Exercise of Freedom of
Expression?" (1994), 4 N.J.C.L. 169, Mr. Lepofsky mounts another critical
analysis of the
Irwin Toy
decision, and writes (at p. 192):

Under
[Irwin
Toy's
s. 2
(b) approach], too much human activity is
swept into the embrace of
section 2
(b), with the result that too many cases are
sent on for deliberations under section 1. The ultimate result will not be
greater protection for the freedom of expression. Rather, the result will be
less principled and more unpredictable
Charter

litigation.

For our part, we do not think the words of
Dickson C.J.C.
et al.
in
Irwin Toy
defining the scope of the
s.
2
(b) guarantee were intended to be strictly construed. We do not think that the
effect of their broad, all-encompassing language, and that found in later decisions
of the court, has been to sweep all human activities (other than acts of
criminal violence) that convey or attempt to convey a meaning into the
protection of
s. 2
(b). Any other conclusions would be to make a mockery of the
values underlying freedom of expression (which the court has identified and
adopted), and of the purpose for entrenching this fundamental right in our
Constitution (which the court has also identified and adopted).

We find support for our view in the majority's
car-parking example in
Irwin Toy.
Dickson C.J.C.
et al.
wrote (at
p. 607):

It might be difficult to characterize
certain day-to-day tasks, like parking a car, as having expressive content. To
bring such activity within the protected sphere, the plaintiff would have to
show that it was performed to convey a meaning. For example, an unmarried
person might, as part of a public protest, park in a zone reserved for spouses
of government employees in order to express dissatisfaction or outrage at the
chosen method of allocating a limited resource. If that person could
demonstrate that his activity did in fact have expressive content, he would, at
this stage, be within the protected sphere and the
s. 2
(b) challenge would
proceed.

That example makes sense. As Lamer J. (as he
then was) acknowledged in
Reference re: ss. 193 and 195.1(1) (c) of the
Criminal Code
(at p. 111):

Obviously, almost all human activity
combines expressive and physical elements. For example sitting down expresses a
desire not to be standing. Even silence, the apparent antithesis of expression,
can be expressive in the sense that a moment's silence on November 11th conveys
a meaning.

A person who parks his/her car in a no-parking
zone has engaged in activity which has an expressive element: his desire to
bring his car to a stop, and to alight from it. Passers-by will observe and
understand what he is doing. In that sense, "meaning" has been
conveyed. But if that activity has no purpose that involves a public interest,

s. 2
(b) cannot be invoked in his/her challenge to the constitutional validity
of the municipal by-law under which a parking ticket has been issued.
Similarly, the driver who fails to obey a red light will not be entitled to
rely on freedom of expression in his/her attack upon the provisions of the
Highway
Traffic Act.
The point is that those activities do not convey or attempt to
convey meaning falling within the scope of the guarantee under
s. 2
(b); they
have nothing to do with freedom of expression.

This view of the scope of freedom of expression
guarantee under
s. 2
(b) finds support in the comment of Sopinka J., writing for
the majority, in
Butler.
He wrote (at p. 152):

An example of the "purely
physical" activity alluded to in
Irwin, Toy
was that of parking a
car which, if performed as a day-to-day task, cannot be said to have expressive
content. Such purely physical activity may be dis­tinguished from
that form
of activity which we are concerned with in the present appeal which, while
indeed "physical", conveys ideas, opinions, or feelings.

(Emphasis added.) See also the comment of Wilson
J., in her concurring reasons in
Lavigne v. Ontario Public Service Employ­ees
Union
(1991),
1991 CanLII 68 (SCC)
, 81 D.L.R. (4th) 545, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 211, 91 C.L.L.C.
¶14,029. She quoted from
Irwin Toy
(at p. 586):

Freedom of expression was entrenched in our
Constitution ... so as to ensure that everyone can manifest their thoughts,
opinions, beliefs, indeed all expressions of the heart and mind, however
unpopular, distasteful or contrary to the mainstream.

And then observed (also at p. 586):

Even although the court has interpreted
s.
2
(b) in this generous way, it has not so far suggested that any activity which
conveys meaning automatically falls within its compass.

The Supreme Court has never retreated from its
acceptance and endorsement in
Ford v. Quebec
of the values that justify
the
Charter
's fundamental guarantee under
s. 2(b)
. Indeed, we find repeated
references to them in the court's
s. 2
(b) jurisprudence: see, for example,
Irwin
Toy Ltd.
; Reference re: ss. 193 and 195.1(1) (c) of the Criminal Code; Keegstra;

Canada (Canadian Human Rights Commission)
v.
Taylor

(1990),
1990 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, 75
D.L.R. (4th) 577, {1990] 3 S.C.R. 892, 13 C.H.R.R. D/435;
Committee for the
Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada
; Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
v.
Lessard

(1991),
1991 CanLII 49 (SCC)
, 67 C.C.C. (3d) 517, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 421, 9 C.R. (4th) 133;
Butler;
Zundel; Peterborough (City)
v.
Ramsden
(1993),
1993 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, 106 D.L.R. (4th) 233,
[1993] 2 S.C.R. 1084, 23 C.R. (4th) 391; and
Native Women's Assn. of Canada
v.

Canada,
1994 CanLII 27 (SCC)
, [1994] S.C.J. No. 93 (October 27, 1994) [reported 119 D.L.R.
(4th) 224, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 627, 24 C.R.R. (2d) 233].

As we have already seen, in
Keegstra
,
Dickson
C.J.C. described the
s. 2
(b) guarantee as "the linchpin" between
freedom of expression and the political process. It is the political or public
purpose of expressive activity that brings it within the protection of
s. 2
(b).
Protected expression must have a connection, however tenuous that connection
may be, with some public or societal purpose or interest.

In an early
s. 2
(b) decision, McIntyre J. stated
that acts of violence and threats of violence would be outside the protection
of freedom of expression:
Dolphin Delivery
at p. 186. More recently, the
court has said that threats of violence are not excluded:
Keegstra

at p.
26. Those cases were concerned with expressive activity that had a public or
political purpose or interest: the picketing of union members in
Dolphin
Delivery,
and the promo­tion of hatred in
Keegstra
.
Indeed, that is
true of all of the court's
s. 2
(b) decisions. A public, political or social
purpose or interest has always been present. We do not interpret the
obiter
comments
in the court's
s. 2
(b) jurisprudence as determining that threats of violence,
where no such interest is present, are worthy of constitutional protection. An
accused who dragged his victim, a stranger, off the street and raped her,
cannot raise freedom of expression in defence of his act; and we cannot believe
that the court intended by its obiter comments that his threats to rape his
victim would be harboured under
s. 2
(b).

No one has resiled from the proposition that
violence itself does not constitute Charter-protected expression. While the
conduct of the accused did not involve physical violence, it did involve a
violent and wholly unjustified assault upon the character and reputation of the
complainant. She suffered injury which might well be more lasting and serious
than the physical injury of being beaten and bruised. The motivation is the
same whether the violence is to flesh and bone or to the integrity of one's
reputation; it is to inflict an injury which will cause pain. The publications
by the accused go beyond threat of violence. They constitute violence itself.

It is worthy of note that the report of the
Select Committee appointed to consider criminal libel in England, which was
presented to the House of Lords on June 1, 1843, and which led to the passing
of
Lord Campbell's Act,
equated libel with certain other crimes. The
committee concluded that "libel was a crime, as theft was crime, or as
assaulting an individual was crime". If theft and assault are outside the
ambit of freedom of expression — and no one has suggested otherwise — so, too,
should be defamatory libel.

The injurious nature of the accused's
expression, bereft as it is from any redeeming purpose, removes the accused's
conduct from the protection of the
Charter
. His actions simply do not engage
what L'Heureux-Dubé J. identified in
Committee for the
Common­wealth
of

Canada as the court's interpretation of the Charter's basic purpose (at p.
426): "[T]he free exchange of ideas, open debate of public affairs, the
effective working of democratic institutions and the pursuit of knowledge and
truth."

"Libel chill" pervades the arguments
of the accused in this case. In
Zundel,
McLachlin J. expressed concern
for what is at the heart of "libel chill": namely, the difficulty in
distinguishing between "fact" and "opinion", between
truthful speech and false speech. That concern evaporates in the face of the
factual circumstances in this appeal and in
Clemente.
Right-thinking
persons in the community, we are sure, would want to see those kinds of
expression "chilled". To do so, in our view, would not impinge upon
the principles and values which underlie freedom of expression. That is so, not
because the communications of the accused were false (which they were), but
because they have no value.

A recent case before the European Court of Human
Rights,
Jersild y. Denmark
(Case No. 36/1993/431/510; reported in The
Times of London, October 20, 1994), illustrates that it is not necessary to
constitutionally protect all contents of expression in order to eradicate the
libel chill concern. In that case, the conviction of a journalist under
Denmark's penal code for broad­casting racist statements was overturned. The
journalist had produced and had caused to be broadcast a documentary about a
group of young people, called "greenjackets", who espoused racist
views about immigrants and ethnic minorities in Denmark. The documentary
contained portions of his interviews with three greenjacket representatives
containing crude remarks. The court held that the conviction had been a
violation of the journalist's right of freedom of expression under art. 10 of
the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental
Freedoms. The report of the court's decision notes that:

Not only did the press have the task of
imparting such information and ideas: the public also had the right to receive
them. Were it otherwise, the press would be unable to play a vital role of
public watchdog.

Of particular significance to the facts of this
appeal is the conclusion of the court that the racist remarks "in respect
of which the greenjackets were convicted were clearly insulting to members of
the targeted groups and did not enjoy the protection of article 10".

In this very case, the reasons for decision of
this court, like the article written by the journalist in the
Jersild
decision,
repeat the harmful material initially produced by the accused. Even if the
complainant's name and address were not deleted, the republica­tion would be
entitled to
Charter
protection because the reasons are an integral part of the
democratic process. They serve an educational and informational purpose and
thus fulfil a societal objective. It is not an aberration that the same words
may or may not be deserving of Charter protection, depending upon the context
of their publication. These cases are to be decided on a case-by-case basis.

The facts of a particular case may present the
court with difficult questions: does the distasteful, offensive, even criminal,
expressive activity manifest thoughts, opinions or beliefs; does it raise the
values and interests that are traditionally associated with the free expression
guarantee? McLachlin J., in her concur­ring reasons in
Committee for the
Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada
,
recognized these concerns, but she
reasoned (at p. 451):

... a failure to invest s. 2(b) with
meaningful content reflective of those principles threatens to trivialize the

Charter
guarantee of free expression. For these reasons a threshold test is
required to screen out cases clearly falling outside the free speech guarantee
before reaching the s. 1 analysis.

Our colleague, Twaddle J.A., rightly observes
that these com­ments were made in the context of a case grappling with whether
government property, an air terminal, could be used as the forum in which
freedom of expression might be exercised. But when McLachlin J. speaks of
screening out cases clearly falling outside the free speech guarantee before
going on to a s. 1 analysis, she is referring to content rather than form or
forum. McLachlin J. indicated that where restrictions on the use of government property
are designed to control the content of speech, the infringement of
s. 2
(b) is established.
But where the restrictions are "content neutral" and the aim is to
avoid the undesirable consequences of expression, then the claimant must go on
to establish a violation of
s. 2
(b) by demonstrating that the content of the
expression falls within the ambit of one of the underlying purposes of the
guarantee of free speech. Thus, the screening out of cases before reaching a s.
1 analysis is dependent upon content and freedom of expression is not absolute
in terms of content.

The approach taken by McLachlin J. in
Committee
for the Commonwealth
of Canada v. Canada, albeit in a minority judgment,
enabled her, having found a violation of
s. 2
(b), to return to the strict but
principled s. 1 test which the court enunciated in
R.
v.
Oakes

(1986),

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)

1.
Does the
Charter
protect Mr. Stevens'
right to publish his objectionable materials?

I originally thought this question could be disposed

300

Section 300 of the

300. Every one who publishes a defamatory
libel that he knows is false is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years.

The terms "defamatory libel" and
"publishes" are defined by ss. 298 and 299 of the
Code
as
follows:

298(1) A defamatory libel is matter
published, without lawful justifica­tion or excuse, that is likely to injure
the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule,
or that is designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published.

(2) A defamatory libel may be expressed
directly or by insinuation or irony

(a) in words legibly marked upon any
substance; or

(b) by any object signifying a defamatory
libel otherwise than by words.

299. A person publishes a libel when he

(a) exhibits it in public;

(b) causes it to be read or seen; or

(c)
shows or
delivers it, or causes it to be shown or delivered, with intent that it should
be read or seen by the person whom it defames or by any other person.

Section 300 undoubtedly has the purpose and
effect of restrict­ing free expression by prohibiting, on threat of penal
sanction, the publication of meaningful words. Does it make any difference that
the words are defamatory, untrue and known by the publisher to be untrue? I
think not. In
R.
y.
Zundel, supra,
all members of the Supreme
