which was both false and known to be false.

3.
Is the s. 300 limit justified?

The Charter does not stop society from
protecting its members from harmful words. Thus, in
R.
v.
Butler,
supra,
obscenity laws were upheld in part because "Parliament was
entitled to have a 'reasoned apprehension of harm' resulting from the
desensitization of individuals exposed to materials which depict violence,
cruelty and dehumanization in sexual relations":
per
Sopinka J. at
p. 164. Such protective legislation must, however, be justified under
s. 1
of
the
Charter
.

It is the Crown's position, in this case, that
s. 300 is required to protect the reputation of individuals and, in doing so,
to uphold "respect for the inherent dignity of the human person" and
this country's "commitment to social justice", two of the values
essential to a free and democratic society referred to by Dickson C.J.C. in
R.
v. Oakes

(1986),
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 24 C.C.C. (3d) 321 at p. 346, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200, [1986]

protecting the reputa­tion of individuals is far more important than freedom to
express that which is known to be false and defamatory. She says the only
effect of s. 300 is to limit expressive activity which is not worthy of
protection.

Defence counsel, on the other hand, contends
that the law is vague; that its objective when enacted was not the protection
of reputation, but the maintenance of public order; that this objective is
irrelevant today; that the offence is much wider than is necessary to protect
reputations; and that it creates what he calls "libel chill" for those
who fear prosecution for publishing an unwitting libel.

In order to determine which argument is right,
the court must embark upon what is called a s. 1 analysis. This follows the
form established by the Supreme Court of Canada in
R.
v.
Oakes
,
supra,
and requires us to address three questions:

(i) Is the limit prescribed by law?

(ii) Is the objective for which it was
enacted of sufficient importance to override a
Charter
freedom?

(iii) Are the means chosen to achieve the
objective reasonable and demonstrably justified?

As I turn towards these questions, I recall that
"a mechanistic approach must be avoided":
per
La Forest J. in
United
States of America v. Cotroni
(1989),
1989 CanLII 106 (SCC)
, 48 C.C.C. (3d) 193 at p. 218, [1989] 1

path to the ultimate goal, which is to determine whether the limit on free
expression is reasonable and demonstra­bly justified. In this context, the
content of Mr. Stevens' publica­tions, previously irrelevant, may now be looked
at as they illustrate the nature of the expressive activity which the state
seeks to restrict. The more worthy this activity, the more difficult it is to
justify a limit on it. On the other hand, a limit on activity which is harmful
to another and far removed from the values embodied in the freedom of
expression can more readily be justified.

(i)
Is the limit prescribed
by
law?

Although s. 300 is a duly enacted legislative
provision, Mr. Stevens' counsel contends that its provisions are too vague to

The accusation of vagueness would, I think, be
more properly directed at the general offence of defamatory libel under s. 301.

mens rea
required
includes an intention to defame. Any lack of precision there may be, however,

(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, [1985] 1 S.C.R.
295, that any limit on a
Charter
freedom must have an objective of sufficient
importance to warrant overriding the constitutional guarantee. To have that
degree of importance, the objective must "relate to concerns which are
pressing and substantial":
per
Dickson C.J.C. in
R.
v.
Oakes
,
supra,
at p. 348. In finding the legislative objective of s. 319(2) of the
Code

(banning the wilful promotion of hatred against identifiable groups) to
meet the standard of justification, Dickson C.J.C. for the majority in
R.
v.

Keegstra
, supra,
noted (at p. 45) that it was an objective "of the
utmost importance"; that the banned activity was activity from which
"substantial harm ... can flow"; and that the section had "a
powerfully convincing legislative objective".

The objective to be judged is that of
"those who drafted and enacted the legislation at the time":
per
Dickson
J. in
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
, supra,
at p. 417. The court
"cannot assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived
current utility of the impugned provision":
per
McLachlin J. for
the majority in
R.
v.
Zundel, supra,
at p. 513.

This is not an easy case in which to identify
those who drafted and enacted the impugned law. Although it is found in the
present
Code,
the law has been carried forward in almost unaltered form
(save as to penalty) since the first
Criminal Code

was enacted in 1892.
Even then, that enactment was no more than a codification of a law first
adopted by the Canadian Parliament in 1874 (an "Act respecting the Crime
of Libel", S.C. 1874, c. 38), and revised and re-enacted in 1886 (an
"Act respecting Libel", R.S.C. 1886, c. 163).

The 1874 legislation was not original. It merely
adopted the law of England as it had existed at the time of confederation. The
objective of the 1874 legislation appears to have been, as its preamble
asserts, to make the law respecting the crime of libel "uniform throughout
all portions of Canada".

The preamble to the 1874 legislation also
asserted that the statute's purpose was "for the better protection of
private character, and for more effectually securing the liberty of the press, and
for better preventing abuses in exercising the said liberty", but these
words had been written before. They were reproduced verbatim from the preamble
to the United Kingdom statute commonly known as
Lord Campbell's Act, 1843
(U.K.),
c. 96). That statute substantially modified the common law of
criminal libel and its provisions were prominent in the 1874 Canadian
legislation.

The objective of the Canadian Parliament in
enacting the law of 1874 (including the forerunner of what is now s. 300 of the

Code)
was solely, it seems to me, to ensure that the English law of
criminal libel was adopted for application throughout Canada. I have neither
found nor been directed to anything which suggests that, in those early days
following Confederation, Parliament did what it would do now, separately
consider the appropriateness of the legislation. Indeed, even when codification
occurred in 1892, the provisions relating to the crime of libel were taken from
a
Draft Code
prepared in England. According to the Law Reform Commission
of Canada, Working Paper No. 35, at p. 5; "What was believed to be the
position of the crime of defamatory libel at common law, as altered by the
English statutory changes, was incorporated into the English
Draft Code,
which,
in turn, was adopted almost verbatim by the first Canadian
Criminal Code
of
1892." The English
Draft Code,
ironically perhaps, was never
enacted.

Support for this view that the Canadian
Parliament's objective was to ensure that the English law was adopted for
application throughout Canada is found in the only surviving record of the
parliamentary debates of 1874, namely, the so-called "Scrapbook
Debates" which are in the Library of Parliament. These may be referred to
because we are concerned with the objective of the legislation rather than its
construction: see, e.g.,
R. v. Morgentaler
(1993),
1993 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 85 C.C.C. (3d) 118 at
p. 133, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 537, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 463,
per
Sopinka J.
Caution must be exercised, of course, in the use of these debates, particularly
because the views of one parliamentarian are not necessarily those of
Parliament, but they, like the reports of select committees and other reliable
sources of historical information, do have a value in the search for parliamen­tary
motivation.

Referring then to the Scrapbook Debates, the
following appears in a clipping from the Senate debates of April 29, 1874:

CRIMINAL LIBEL BILL

MR. KAULBACK, in
moving the second reading of the Criminal Libel Bill, gave a historical sketch
of the bill. The law, he said, had been in existence in England over thirty
years, and had been in existence in Ontario, and he thought, it should be now adopted
by the whole Dominion ...

MR. DICKEY concurred
in the general aim and scope of the bill.

MR. MILLER was
fully convinced the bill was wanted.

MR. PENNY said that
the fact of the whole of that Act having been on the English statute book for
over thirty years was a
prima facie
proof that it was a good one.

In those circumstances, I think the objectives
of the law of England pertaining to criminal libel must be attributed to the
Canadian Parliament. It thus becomes necessary to ascertain what those
objectives were and particularly those of the United Kingdom Parliament in
enacting s. 4 of
Lord Campbell's Act, 1843,
the equivalent of the
present s. 300 of the
Code.

The common law offence of defamatory libel
appears to have had its origins in the Court of Star Chamber. The wrong of
defamation had previously been recognized in England and, in the case of libels
affecting public figures, criminalized. But, as far as I can tell, it was in
the Star Chamber that the crime, as we now know it, was first developed.

The objective of the Star Chamber in creating
the offence may be gleaned from the following passages from the report of
Case
de Libellis Famosis
(1606),
5 Co. Rep. 125
a,
77 E.R. 250 (Star Chamber) at
p. 251
:

If it
(a
libel)
be against a private man it deserves a severe punishment,
for
although the libel be made against one, yet it incites all those of the same
family, kindred, or society to revenge, and so tends
per consequens
to
quarrels and breach of the peace, and may be the cause of shedding of blood,
and of great inconvenience ..

Although the private man ... be dead al
the time of the making of the libel, yet it is punishable;
for it stirs up others of the same family, blood, or society, to revenge,
and to break the peace ...

. and of such nature is libelling, it is
secret and robs a man of his good name, which ought to be more precious to him
than his life ... and therefore when the offender is known, he ought to be
severely punished.

(Emphasis in the original text.)

Although there is a reference to the protection
of the victim's good name, the thrust of the policy enunciated by the Court of
Star Chamber was to penalize libel on the ground that it tended to cause a
breach of the peace by inciting the victim, or his family or friends, to seek
revenge. The crime of libel survived the abolition of the Court of Star
Chamber, in 1641: jurisdiction with respect to it was exercised by the Court of
King's Bench. As far as I can tell, however, the policy objectives remained the
same.

The Court of King's Bench not only recognized it
as an offence to publish a libel about the living, but also one about the dead
(see, e.g.,
R.
v.
Topham
(1791), 4 T.R. 126, 100 E.R. 931
), and
one about a definable group (see,
e.g. R.
v.
Osborn
(1732), 2
Barn. K.B. 138 at p. 166, 94 E.R. 40
G at p. 425, in which a libel about
"certain Jews" in a particular community was the subject of
prosecution, and
Gathercole Case
(1838), 2 Lew. C.C. 237, 168 E.R. 1140
,
in which a reference to a particular nunnery as a house of prostitution
resulted in a prosecution). The most likely rationale for these offences was
the maintenance of public peace.

Other than the brief reference in
Case de Libellis
Farnosis, supra,
to a libel robbing a man of his good name, and to the
remarks of Henry Brougham, later Lord Chancellor, to which I shortly will
refer, I have found little in legal literature to suggest that the protection
of reputation was an objective of the pre-1843 criminal law. This was more the
objective of the civil law which covered slander as well as libel and, by
allowing truth as a defence, enabled a successful plaintiff to assert
positively that the imputa­tion against his character had been false.

Truth was no defence to a criminal libel. The
saying was: "The greater the truth, the greater the libel." This had
two conse­quences of note. The press was circumscribed in what it could publish
about a rogue or even a public figure whose conduct deserved reproof. And
victims of the crime were sometimes further outraged by the assertion of a
libeller that, if only the law had allowed it, he could have proved the truth
of his defamatory statement.

The first contradiction I have found of the
law's objective being the maintenance of public peace is contained in a speech
delivered by Henry Brougham, Lord Chancellor from 1830 to 1834, when a member
of the House of Commons in 1816. Speaking on a motion to approve a "Bill
for Securing the Liberty of the Press", he said:

In case of libel the legal fiction
proceeded on the idea that character was nothing, and that the tendency to a
breach of the peace was everything; but why adhere to such a fallacy? Why not
admit that character was of some value, that it was property which deserved
protection ... The robbery of our good name, which was dearer to us than any
other species of possessions, deserved a certain degree of punishment, although
the act had no tendency to create tumult or a breach of the peace.

(The Parliamentary Debates, 1816, vol. 34, p.
389.)

Mr. Brougham then went on to point out that the
punishment for an actual breach of the peace was frequently much less severe
than that for publishing a libel. He said:

Here the tendency to crime was punished
more heavily than the crime itself. Did not the absurd inference like this show
the fallacy of the premises from which it was legitimately drawn, and
consequently that a breach of the peace was not the true ground of proceeding
in cases of libel?

By 1843, there was sufficient clamour for the
law to change to warrant at least a review of the existing law. Lord Campbell
(later Chief Justice of the Queen's Bench, and later still Lord Chancellor)
consequently moved in the House of Lords on February 13, 1843, for the appointment
of a select committee to look into the law of defamation, both criminal and
civil. In the course of his speech, he said:

We are told that the essence of the offence
consists in its tendency to produce a breach of the peace—which is as great
whether the charge be true or false; and indeed, if the principle were just,
the legitimate consequence is, "that the greater the truth, the greater
the libel;" for it has been justly observed that many people despise what
is palpably false, and resent what has the appearance of probability. But I
regard this reason for making libel a criminal offence a contemptible fiction.
Libel is an offence in the same manner that theft is an offence; because it
deprives a citizen of that which he is entitled to enjoy, and which the good of
society requires should be protected by penal sanctions. Is it really criminal
to calumniate a bishop or a judge, or a friendless woman, because it is feared
they would break the peace by horse-whipping the libeller?

(Hansard's Parliamentary Debates, 3rd Series,
vol. 66, p. 402).

A select committee of the House of Lords,
chaired by Lord Campbell, was consequently appointed. The report of the commit­tee
is reproduced in the Journals of the House of Lords (1843), V.75, app. No. 3,
pp. 34
et seq.
Its recommendations, with some exceptions, were
incorporated into
Lord Campbell's Act.

The Act amended the law of criminal libel in two
major respects. It made truth a defence so long as the publication was also for
the public benefit and, by s. 4, it created a new offence, sometimes referred
to as aggravated libel, which was the forerunner of what is now s. 300 of the
Canadian
Criminal Code.

The objective of making truth a defence, even in
limited circumstances, is readily identifiable. It was to remove an intolera­ble
limit on free speech and, to use the words of the preamble, "for the
better protection of private character". It achieved this latter objective
by making it more difficult for a libeller to compound his offence by claiming
that, but for the law, he could have proved the truth of what he had written.

In requiring that a truthful publication also be
for the public benefit, Parliament was, I think, aiming to protect those whom
even the truth could harm unfairly. An example given by the select committee
illustrates this. A young woman who has a child out of wedlock (a transgression
in those days) moves to a new town and lives in an upright manner for several
decades, only to have her earlier indiscretion brought to light for no reason
other than to create a scandal. In those circumstances, it was thought, the
publisher of the indiscretion should not be able to escape punishment by
relying on the truth.

More obscure is the objective of creating the
more serious offence of publishing a defamatory libel which the publisher knows
to be false. A distinction between a libel which, though true, was not
published for the public benefit, and one which was false, would have been
understandable, but why impose on the prosecu­tion the very heavy burden of proving
the publisher's knowledge of the falsity? To answer that question, reference
must be made to the proceedings before the select committee.

Witnesses who appeared before the committee
advised against the creation of a distinct offence of publishing a false libel.
One such witness, Thomas Starkie, a renowned expert in the law of defamation,
testified (at p. 51 of the committee's report):

I think there may be a difficulty in having
Two Offences charged in separate Counts, the one consisting in the malicious
Publication of a Libel, and the other the malicious Publication of a false
Libel. There are very few who would like to prosecute at all, who could not
prosecute for a false Libel, because it would be a sort of admission, if they
did, that the Libel was true.

Henry Kerr, a member of the Criminal Law
Commission, warned the committee
(ibid.,
p. 108):

[I]f you make Two Forms of Indictment, and
Two Special Crimes, one in which the Truth is to be proved, and the other not,
Persons would be deterred from prosecuting, either from an Apprehension, even
if the Libel were false, that they might not be able to meet the Evidence
adduced by the Libeller in support of the Truth of his Libel, or from a
Disinclination, if the Libel were True, to the milder Mode of Proceeding, which
in fact would be an Admission of the Libel ..

The committee was none the less concerned that
the mainte­nance of a single category of criminal libel did not do enough to
protect the character of persons from false libels. It specifically inquired of
Thomas Starkie
(ibid.,
p. 52) whether it was true that the law provided
no special punishment for "the specific offence of a wilful and false
Imputation upon the Character of a Party". Starkie replied that this was
so and "that I take to be the great Defect".

It may be that the genesis of the offence of
publishing a libel known to be false can be found in that exchange. It may also
be that the principal targets of the committee's recommendation to create that
offence were the "disreputable weekly Newspapers" who were such
"Pests of Society"
(ibid.,
p. 35), the hope being that those
mischievous merchants of libel and scandal would be caught in the net of the
new offence. In any event, I think it clear that the objective of the committee
was not the preservation of the peace, but the protection of reputation.

There was particular advantage in requiring the
prosecutor of an aggravated libel charge to prove the libeller's knowledge of
falsity. A failure to prove this knowledge would not justify a conclusion that
the libel was true. In other words (those of Gary Dolovich, research officer to
the court), by making the holes in the new offence's net wide enough only to
catch the largest and, therefore, smelliest fish, the committee was affording
the fisher­man the opportunity of blaming his lack of a catch on the holes in
his net.

That the purpose of establishing this new
category was the protection of reputation is also supported by Lord Campbell's
closing remarks to the committee. He said (at p. 105):

It seems to me that the Ground upon which
it is said that private Defamation is criminal is wholly fallacious. The Ground
generally alleged is that it leads to a Breach of the Peace. I do not think
that this is so either on Principle or in Practice, On Principle, I think that
Defamation is a crime like Theft or Battery of the Person; It is doing an
Injury to a Member of Society, who is entitled to the Protection of the Law,
and the Person who perpetrates that Injury ought to be punished as an Example
to others to prevent a repetition of the Offence. In Practice Prosecutions for
Libel are uniformly instituted and conducted by the Party injured, and merely
with a view of vindicating the Character of the Party injured, or of having
Revenge upon the Libeller, and riot in the remotest Degree with any view to the
Protection of the public Peace.

The report of the select committee was laid upon
the table in the House of Lords on June 1, 1843. I will spare my readers the
task of reading what was said on that occasion (see Hansard's Parliamen­tary
Debates, 3rd Series, vol. 69, pp. 1233
et seq.),
the remarks mainly
being repetitious of what Lord Campbell had said earlier, but I will refer
briefly to the debates in the House of Commons when the bill reached there.
Contrary to the usual practice, a verbatim report of these debates is not found
in Hansard's Parliamentary Debates, 1843, 3rd Series, vol. 71, but rather a
review of what various members said. The following is found at p. 870:

The knowledge of the falsehood will often
show greater malice in the libeller, and will warrant the infliction of greater
punishment. Hitherto, as is well known, the criminal branch of the law of libel
has been based upon an altogether different principle — an imaginary principle
— that of the tend­ency of libels to provide breaches of the peace. I think
public opinion has been too unequivocally pronounced upon this fundamental
principle for libel, to require that the time of the House be taken up by
proving that it is no more nor less than a fiction, that it is also a very
inappropriate fiction, and it leads to much practical mischief.

It is logically difficult to attribute to the
United Kingdom Parliament in enacting s. 4 of
Lord Campbell's Act
a
different objective than that stated by Lord Campbell himself and con­firmed by
the quoted passage from the House of Commons debates. So long as the objective
was the maintenance of peace, the old saying "the greater the truth, the
greater the libel" was apt. Once it became "the greater the lie, the
greater the libel", another objective had to be that in mind.

None the less, the view of libel as a crime
against the peace remained prevalent throughout the 19th century. Thus, in
R.

v.
Holbrook
(1878), 4 Q.B.D. 42
, Lush J. said (at p. 46) that the
law ranked libel among criminal offences "because of its supposed tendency
to arouse angry passion, provoke revenge, and thus endanger the public
peace". And the learned author, W. Odgers, in An
Outline of the Law of
Libel
(London: MacMillan & Co. Ltd., 1897), wrote (at p. 178) that
libel had been criminalized to protect the state's interest

…in repressing all such libels and lampoons
as are calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, or which for any other
reason tend to disturb the civil order and harmony of society.

Indeed, a revised version of Thomas Starkie's
text,
The Law of Slander and Libel,
6th ed. (London: William Clowes
& Sons Ltd., 1897) (edited by Henry Folkard), contains the following
statement (at p. 167):

Libel is ranked among criminal offences
because of its supposed tendency to arouse angry passions, to provoke revenge,
quarrels, duels, and assaults; and thereby to endanger public peace.

Small wonder then, when the text originally
written by the select committee's expert propounds this view, that it prevailed
as the rationale for criminal libel for most of the 20th century. What everyone
holding this view must have overlooked was the footnote to the last-quoted
passage:

This is the ground upon which, by the law
of England, the defamation of private individuals is said to constitute a
criminal offence. It is, however, very questionable whether this ground is not
too narrow, if not altogether fallacious. The true principle would seem to be,
that a libel on a private individual should be punished as a criminal offence
for the protection of
individual character, or for reputation's sake, as
well as for the preservation of public peace;
both the private individual
and the public would then be protected, upon the same principles as in the
cases of assault and battery.

(Emphasis in original.)

The significance of the crime's tendency to
cause a breach of the peace seems to have lessened somewhat in the 20th
century. Thus, in
R.
v.
Wicks
(1936), 25 Cr. App. R. 168, [1936]
1 All E.R. 384
, the English Court of Criminal Appeal held that, whatever the
original objective may have been, the tendency of a libel to cause a breach of
the peace was not an essential element of the offence. And in
Gleaves
v.

Deakin,
[1980] A.C. 477, [1979] 2 All E.R. 497 (H.L.)
, their Lordships said
that if a tendency to cause a breach of the peace had ever been an element of
the offence, it had ceased to be.

Having regard to the history of the offence as I
have outlined it and particularly to the proceedings before the select
committee, I am of the view that
Lord Campbell's
Act might be viewed as
the watershed which divides the days when the law's objective was the
maintenance of peace and those when the law's objective was primarily the
protection of reputation. And in particular, the objective of s. 4 of
Lord
Campbell's Act
was the protection of reputation from wilful and false
attack. I think this new objective was that which the Canadian Parliament had
in mind when it adopted and later codified the English law of criminal libel.
This view is supported by the placement of what is now s. 300 in that part of
the 1892
Code
dealing with "Offences Against the Person and
Reputation".

I turn now to a consideration of whether this
objective is of sufficient importance to warrant overriding the freedom of
expression.

Although we look to the origin of a law for its
objective, we must consider its importance in the context of the present time.
Thus, in
R.
v.
Zundel, supra,
McLachlin J., in dealing with a
section of the
Code
which, like s. 300, had been in the original
Code

of 1892 in substantially the same form, noted the Law Reform Commission's
recommendation that it be repealed and considered whether, in light of this,
the section remained one directed at a pressing and substantial social concern.

The social concern we are dealing with in the
present case is the loss of individual reputation as a result of wilful and
false attack. There have been laws to meet this concern for centuries, and they
continue to exist in most, if not all, civilized societies. Mr. Stevens does
not really say that laws intended to protect reputation are not of importance.
His position is that, contrary to what I find, the objective of the particular
law he attacks was the maintenance of public peace. Once the true objective is
identified, it is difficult to see how anyone could seriously suggest that the
objective of protecting individual reputation from wilful and false attack is
not pressing and substantial in our society. Anyone who doubts this need only
consider the facts of the present case.

It is true that the Law Reform Commission of
Canada and the English Law Commission have recommended abolition of the existing
crimes involving the publication of defamatory libels (see Working Paper No.
35, and "Report on Criminal Libel": Law Commission, No. 149, 1985,
respectively), but neither did so on the ground that the protection of
reputation was unimportant. The Canadian Commission was of the view that the
protection of reputation was an objective which was adequately met by the civil
law whilst the English Commission thought that that was so for all but the most
egregious libels. To cover them, the English Commission recommended the
creation of a new offence somewhat more certain in its scope than the existing
offence of publishing a libel known to be false.

The reasoning of the two commissions does raise
a question as to whether it is necessary to invoke the criminal law for the
protection of reputation and, if it is, a further question as to whether the
existing offence under s. 300 of the
Code
goes too far. These questions,
however, relate to the means by which the objective should be met rather than
its importance. The proper place to consider the suitability of the means by
which the protection of reputation is achieved is, in my view, under the
proportionality test.

It is sufficient to take us to the next stage of
the analysis that I find the social concern for the reputation of individuals
to be pressing and substantial. This I most certainly do.

(iii)
Are the means chosen reasonable and
demonstrably justified?

Although the seminal statement of the
proportionality test is that of Dickson C.J.C. in
R. v. Oakes
, supra,
at
pp. 348-9, I will quote from the simpler version offered by Sopinka
J.
in

R.
v.
Butler, supra,
at p. 161:

The proportionality requirement has three
aspects:

(1) the existence of a rational connection
between the impugned measures and the objective;

(2) minimal impairment of the right or
freedom; and

(3) a proper balance between the effects of
the limiting measures and the legislative objective.

(1)
Rational connection

It is evident from the report of Lord Campbell's
committee that it carefully designed what became s. 4 of the English
legislation (and what is now s. 300 of our
Code)
to meet the objective
it had in mind. I cannot think of a more rational way to protect the reputation
of individuals from wilful and false attack than the creation of the aggravated
offence crafted by the committee. It is narrowly defined and catches only the
most odious offenders. Yet it does offer substantial protection by deterring
those very offenders from committing their outrageous offences. The impugned
measure is thus rationally connected to its objective.

(2)
Minimal impairment

The first question under minimal impairment is
whether a law criminalizing libel is necessary. The protection of reputation is
to a large extent achieved by the civil law of defamation which not only
compensates for harm clone to reputation — often generously — but also provides
relief by way of injunction against repetition of a libel.

In its Working Paper No. 35, the Law Reform
Commission of Canada considered the extent, if any, to which the offence of
criminal defamatory libel should be retained. It began by quoting with approval
from the Department of Justice's argument in
The Criminal Law in Canadian
Society
(Ottawa: Government of Canada, 1982), where it was said (at pp.
52-3):

[T]he criminal law should be employed to
deal only with that conduct for which other means of social control are
inadequate or inappropriate, and in a manner which interferes with individual
rights and freedoms only to the extent necessary for the attainment of its
purpose.

The minimal impairment approach took the
commission to the consideration of a number of factors. They noted the crime's
infrequency of use (Working Paper No. 35, pp. 47-9); the recogni­tion in other
jurisdictions of the need to reform the crime of defamatory libel where based
on English law
(ibid.,
pp. 50-1); the adequacy of the civil remedy
(ibid.,

pp. 51-3); the doubtful effect of criminal sanctions as a deterrent
(ibid.,

pp. 53-4); and the limited usefulness of a restricted crime of defamation
(ibid.,

pp. 55-9).

The commission concluded
(ibid.,
pp.
59-60):

Undoubtedly, reputation is a fundamental
value in our society. An attack upon reputation may well result in serious
consequences to the victim. Let us be frank. Deliberate character
assassinations ought not to be tolerated by society. None the less, as we have
emphasized throughout this Paper, the criminal law must be used with restraint.
For reasons previously explored at some length, we do not feel that a crime of
defamation would be able to do better that which is already done by the civil
law of defamation. Nor would it seem to be an effective deterrent. Therefore,
we do not feel that a crime of defamation could make a substantial contribution
in dealing with the problem of defamatory publications in our society.
Accordingly, we recom­mend that our
Criminal
Code
should contain no
crime of defamation, even in a restricted form.

The English Law Commission reached a similar
conclusion with respect to the criminal law of libel as it exists today:
"Report on Criminal Libel",
supra.
None the less, the English
Commission did recommend the creation of a new offence somewhat more certain in
its scope, but essentially similar to the English equivalent of the offence
under s. 300 of our
Code.
It recom­mended
(ibid.,
p. 60) that
"the offence would penalize anyone who communicated to any person false
information which was seriously defamatory of another, knowing or believing
that it was false and that it was seriously defamatory".

In support of the new offence, the English
Commission made use of the following arguments:

(a) The consequences for the victim of a
defamatory statement may be far more serious and long lasting than those of
other acts, such as an assault, or theft, which are accepted as criminal
offences.

(b) If damage to reputation is done
intentionally and with knowledge that a statement is false, then the state of mind
and blameworthiness of the maker are no different in character from the person
who deliberately assaults another or damages his property.

(c) There may also be damage caused to the
public interest: the person defamed may be hampered in performing services or
functions of public importance.

(d) A gravely damaging libel may be published
which the victim cannot afford to ignore, but cannot afford to fight due to the
prohibitive cost of litigation.

(e) Although the present crime is very little
used, it may act as a deterrent, the total removal of which may increase the
incidence of outrageous libels; and

(f) effective means can be found to ensure
that prosecutions are only pursued in clear cases where there is an undoubted
public interest.

I agree with the Canadian Law Reform Commission
that "deliberate character assassinations ought not to be tolerated by
society". As to the need for criminal sanctions for such conduct, I prefer
the reasoning of the English Law Commission. In a commentary on that
commission's Working Paper No. 84, "Crimi­nal Law, Criminal Libel"
(London: Her Majesty's Stationery Office, 1982) and criticism of it, J.R.
Spencer (a fellow of Selwyn College, Cambridge) wrote ([1983] Crim. L.R. 524 at
pp. 527-8):

[Iit is nonsense to say that "the civil
remedy for libel, when invoked, is in fact effective ...". First, the
civil remedy cannot be invoked. Defamation actions have to be brought in the
High Court. They are prodigiously expensive ... .
Consequently, only the super-rich can use the civil remedy, unless the
defendant happens himself to be rich enough to be able to pay costs if he
loses. ... So we must either have a criminal offence, or let the worst of
libellers go free.

The learned author illustrates his point by
reference to some cases where he considered a criminal sanction necessary (at
p. 527):

In
Penketh
((1982), 145 J.P.N. 56),
a widow with a young child heard a broadcast in which a charitable appeal was
made for a pen-friend for D. She wrote to D who bombarded her with letters,
until she decided to end the correspondence. So he got his own back by writing
to the son's headmaster stating that he was the natural father of the child. On
pleading guilty to criminal libel he was put on probation on condition that he
stopped libelling her and left her alone. He did not, and eventually went to
prison for breach of the probation order. In
Fell (The Times,
February
14, 1976), D, who was upset that his relationship with a married woman had
ended, sprayed offensive libels about her in public places all over the town
... ; the woman was so upset that she attempted to commit suicide. In
Leigh
(The Times,
March 9, 1971), D, who was accused of fraud, sought to
discredit the police sergeant in charge of the investigation by printing 5,000
handbills and a number of posters accusing him of being persistently drunk, and
engaging five men to distribute them.... And going back still further, there
was
Greenhouse (The Times,
May 12, 1887), who coveted his superior's
job, and in the hope of relieving him of it, sought to get him the sack by
putting about the story that he had been indecently assaulting little girls.

And now we have this present case. I cannot
think of a better example of defamation which cries out for a criminal
sanction. To quote J.R. Spencer once again (at p. 528): "What is need
against the deliberate character assassin is neither damages, nor an
injunction, but punishment for what he has done — as a deterrent both for him
and for others like him — or a hospital order or suchlike if he turns out to be
mad rather than bad."

If, then, criminal sanctions are required for
cases such as this, does s. 300 impair the freedom of expression as little as
possible or should we insist that, if Parliament wishes to criminalize the most
outrageous libels, it confine the offence to one which, like that recommended
by the English Law Commission, is more narrowly defined?

The English Law Commission is a body which
proposes reform. Naturally, in proposing reform, the commission looks for the
ideal. This is to be contrasted with the function of a Canadian court when
testing the constitutionality of an existing measure. As the Supreme Court of
Canada has said on more than one occasion (see, e.g.,
R.
v.
Edwards
Books & Arts Ltd.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 385 at pp. 435-6, 35 D.L.R.
(4th) 1, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713,
per
Dickson C.J.C., and
Reference re: ss.
193 and 195.1(1)(c) of the Criminal Code (Man.), supra,
also
per
Dickson
C.J.C. at pp. 75-6), the function of a Canadian court in those circumstances is
not to insist on perfection. The question is not whether Parliament could have
found a better way in which to achieve its objective, but whether the way
chosen by Parliament is reasonable.

We must also bear in mind that not all
Charter

infringements are equally serious. Although the value of the freedom of
expression is extremely high in the abstract, and in many ways in which it is
exercised, its value plummets like the temperature in a Winnipeg winter when it
is exercised for such base purposes as the depiction of dehumanizing scenes of
sexual exploitation (see
R.
v.
Butler, supra),
and the wilful
incitement of hatred against identifiable groups (see
R.
y.
Keegstra,
supra).
The value of freedom to tell defamatory lies about another person
falls pretty close to that bottom.

Not only is it easier to justify impairment of a

Charter
right or freedom where the impairment only affects a low-valued
exercise of the right or freedom, but it is also easier to do so where the
objective of the impugned law has itself a high value. Thus, a ban on the
publication of a report on court proceedings is easier to justify where the
purpose is to enable an accused to obtain a fair trial than it would be if the
ban was intended as a form of censorship. In this case, the value of a person's
reputation is very high indeed. Shakespeare put its value in these terms:
"Who steals my purse steals trash ... But he that filches from me my good
name ... makes me poor indeed"
(Othello,
III (iii), 157-61, Iago).

Keeping these preliminary observations in mind,
I now turn to the arguments which assert that s. 300 involves more than minimal
impairment:

That the offence encompasses unintentional
defamations

The
Code
does not expressly provide that
an intention to defame is an element of the offence. None the less, L. Giesbrecht
Prov. Ct. J., in her very thorough judgment, found it to be so and counsel for
the Attorney-General urges us to agree.

At the outset, I remind myself that we are
dealing only with the statutory offence of publishing a defamatory libel that
is known to be false. We must, therefore, exercise care in considering English
authorities which deal with other forms of criminal libel and which do so
without regard to
Charter
values which now govern the construction of Canadian
statutes.

Having expressed that caution, I none the less
will refer to some English authorities decided or written subsequent to the
enact­ment of Fox's
Libel Act, 1792 (U.K.),
c. 60, by which
responsibility for determining whether a publication amounted to a libel was
passed from judge to jury. Thereafter, direction as to the
mens rea
required
for the offence had to be given to the jury. This fact distinguished those
cases decided before that date from those that follow.

In
R.
v.
Lord Abingdon
(1794), 1
Esp. 226 at p. 228, 170 E.R. 337 at p. 338,
Lord Kenyon, Chief Justice of the
King's Bench, was reported as saying: "That in order to constitute a
libel, the mind must be in fault, and shew a malicious intent to defame, for,
if published inadvertently, it would not be a libel;"

The reliability of reports by Isaac Espinasse is
sometimes open to doubt. In
Whyman v. Garth
(1853), 22 L.J. Ex. 316,
when counsel relied on a case reported by Mr. Espinasse, Chief Baron Pollock
remarked: "It used to be said that Mr. Espinasse heard
one
half of the
cases and reported the
other
half." That is certainly not so in
Lord
Abingdon's
case, however, as the report goes on to quote the other half of
Lord Kenyon's remarks [at p. 228 Esp., p. 338 E.R.]:

... but where a libellous publication
appeared unexplained by any evidence, the jury should judge from the overt act,
and where the publication contained a charge slanderous in its nature, should
from thence infer that the intention was malicious.

The second half of Lord Kenyon's remarks perhaps
explains why in many English cases an intention to defame was not always
expressly referred to or, if referred to, was treated as a fact not requiring
proof. The presumption that a person intends the natural consequences of his or
her actions was seen as a legal one. It was not until the passage of the
Criminal
Justice Act, 1967 (U.K.),
c. 80, s. 8, that this presumption was
unmistakably rele­gated to an inference of fact which a jury might, but need
not, make. It, therefore, followed that a person who was found to have published
clearly defamatory material was presumed to have intended to defame the victim.

Thus, in
R.
v.
Harvey and Chapman
(1823),
2 B. & C. 257 at p. 259, 107 E.R. 379 at p. 380,
the Court of King's Bench
approved an instruction given to the jury by Abbott C.J.K.B. which was in the
following terms:

"The man who publishes slanderous
matter, in its nature calculated to defame ... another, must be presumed to
have intended to do that which the publication is calculated to bring about,
unless he can shew the contrary; and it is for him to shew the contrary."

Other cases to the same effect are
R.
v.
Creevey

(1813), 1 M. & S. 273, 105 E.R. 102
, and
R.
v.
Burdett
(1820),
4 B. & Ald. 95, 106 E.R. 873
. On the other hand, in
R. v. Reeves
(1796),
Peake Add. Cas. 84, 170 E.R. 202
, it was held that it was for the jury to
consider whether a libel had been published with criminal intent. And in
R.
v.

Holbrook, supra,
the following statements of the law are to be found:

(i)
per
Lush J., at p. 50:

... I think the jury ought to be told, in
this as in every other case, that criminal intention is not to be presumed, but
is to be proved ...

(i
i) per
Cockburn C.J., at p. 59:

... I cannot but think, of the fundamental
principle that to constitute guilt there must be a mens rea, an intention to
violate the law.

It should be noted, however, that in
R.
v.

Holbrook
the issue was whether the proprietors of a newspaper had
authorized the publication of a libel by their editor. This may explain why the
criminal intention could not be presumed from the publication of defamatory
material.

The case of
R.
y
Munslow,
[1895] 1
Q.B. 758
, is often cited as supporting the proposition that malice (or
"intent to defame" as we might prefer to call it) was not an
essential element of ordinary criminal libel. That was certainly the view of
Sir William Holds-worth ("Defamation in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth
Centuries" (1925), XLI Law Q. Rev. 13 at p. 28), and of the Canadian Law
Reform Commission (Working Paper No. 35, footnote 59). I, on the other hand,
prefer the view expressed by L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J., when she said [at p.
137 C.C.C.]:

The court in that case was concerned with
the omission of the word "maliciously" in the indictment charging
libel under
Lord Campbell's Act, 1843,
s. 5. The court held that an
averment of malice was unnecessary at common law and, therefore, the indictment
was good. The case is riddled with references to the law of inferring malice
from the fact of publication, and to the presumption of intention as to the
probable consequences of one's actions. But Lord Russell also said, at p. 762:
"No doubt
the law implies malice
from the publication of defamatory
matter; but
that implication,
as I have already said, may
be
rebutted"
(emphasis added).

The preponderance of English case law at the end
of the 19th century seems, therefore, to favour the view that malice, or intent
to defame, was indeed an ingredient of criminal libel, albeit a state of mind
which might be presumed from the clearly defamatory nature of the publication. This,
no doubt, accounts for the views expressed by such learned authors as Sir James
Stephen and Glanville Williams. In his
History
of
the
Criminal Law
of
England,
vol. 2 (London, MacMillan &
Co., 1883), ch. 24, at pp. 358 and 359), Sir James Stephen wrote:

The effect of the Libel Act (Fox's) and of
the discussions which led to it, was thus to embody in the definition of the
crime of seditious libel the existence of some kind of
bad intention on the part of the offender ... [T]he Libel Act does not say whether
the averments as to the specific intentions of the defendant in such cases are
or are not material. It no doubt, however, assumes them to be so, and the
law
has ever since been administered upon the supposition that they are.

(Emphasis added.)

Glanville Williams in his work
Criminal Law,
The General Part,
2nd ed. (London: Stevens & Sons Limited, 1961), wrote
(at p. 67): "Libel requires
mens rea
at least in the sense that the
defen­dant ... must have intended to defame, or been reckless as to the defamatory
meaning of his words."

Curiously enough, as it turns out, Glanville
Williams also stated
(ibid.,
p.71): "[B]lasphemy, has long been
settled to be a crime requiring a certain kind of wrongful intention." Not
so, said a slender majority of the House of Lords in
R.
v.
Lemon,
[1979]
A.C. 617, [1979] 1 All E.R. 898
(H.L.(E.)). This decision, which fortunately
does not bind us, lacks even persuasive authority, in my respectful view, when
it is considered against the background I have referred to and in the light of
the severe criticism it received from academic quarters. L. Giesbrecht Prov.
Ct. J. seems to have captured the essence of that criticism when she referred
to the passage from J. R. Spencer's article, "Blasphemous Libel Resur­rected
— Gay News and Grim Tidings", [1979] 38 Camb. L.J. 245, in which he wrote
(at p. 251): "[T]he legal clock seems to have run backwards to 1792 in all
areas of criminal libel."

It is perhaps paradoxical that, having just
rejected the decision in
R. v. Lemon,
I should now begin my
consideration of the meaning to be given to the Canadian statutory measure by
reference to another decision of the House of Lords. In
Sweet
v.
Parsley,

[1970] A.C. 132
(H.L.(E.)), the House was required to decide whether
mens
rea
was an ingredient of a particular statutory offence. Holding that it
was, Lord Reid observed (at p. 148):

Sometimes the words of the section which
creates a particular offence make it clear that mens rea is required in one
form or another. Such cases are quite frequent. But in a very large number of
cases there is no clear indication either way. In such cases there has for
centuries been a presumption that Parliament did not intend to make criminals
of persons who were in no way blameworthy in what they did. This means that whenever
a section is silent as to mens rea there is a presumption that, in order to
give effect to the will of Parliament, we must read in words appropriate to
require mens rea.

That, in my view, is a particularly apt
statement of the law not only in England, but also in Canada: see
Beaver
v.

The Queen

(1957),
1957 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 118 C.C.C. 129, [1957] S.C.R. 531, 26 C.R. 193; and
R.

v.
Sault Ste. Marie
(City)
(1978),
1978 CanLII 11 (SCC)
, 40 C.C.C. (2d) 353 at p. 362, 85 D.L.R.
(3d) 161, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1299, wherein Dickson J. (as he then was) said:

Where the offence is criminal, the Crown
must establish a mental element, namely, that the accused who committed the
prohibited act did so intention­ally or recklessly, with knowledge of the facts
constituting the offence, or with wilful blindness toward them.

Indeed, as was pointed out by Laskin C.J.C. in
R.

v.
Prue
(1979),
1979 CanLII 227 (SCC)
, 46 C.C.C. (2d) 257 at pp. 259-60, 96 D.L.R. (3d)
577, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 547, the very constitutionality of a provision creating a
criminal offence may depend upon the inclusion among its elements of an
appropriate
mens rea.

If that was the state of the law before the

Charter
was enacted, even the more so is it the state of the law today. Now,
not only jurisdictional concerns would dictate reading a
mens rea
require­ment
into a criminal statute; Charter concerns would also do so. Thus, in
Metropolitan
Stores (MTS) Ltd.
v.
Manitoba Food & Commercial Workers, Local 832
(1987),

1987 CanLII 79 (SCC)
, 38 D.L.R. (4th) 321 at p.331, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 110, 87 C.L.L.C. ¶14,015, BeetzJ.,
deliver­ing the judgment of the court, said:

Still another meaning of the
"presumption of constitutionality" is the rule of construction under
which an impugned statute ought to be construed, whenever possible, in such a
way as to make it conform to the Constitution.

This was echoed by Gonthier J. in
R.
v.
Nova
Scotia Pharma­ceutical Society, supra,
where he said (at p. 326):

It must be remembered that if there are two
possible interpretations of a statutory provision, one of which embodies the

Charter
values and the other does not, that which embodies the Charter values
should be adopted.

Statements to like effect are to be found in
Hills
v. Canada (Attorney-General)

(1988),
1988 CanLII 67 (SCC)
, 48 D.L.R. (4th) 193 at pp. 226-7,
[1988] 1 S.C.R. 513, 88 C.L.L.C. ¶14,011, and in
R.
v.
Rube
(1992),

1992 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, 75 C.C.C. (3d) 575n, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 159, [1993] 1 W.W.R. 385. The principle
has been applied by this court in
R. y. Ruston
(1991),
1991 CanLII 2758 (MB CA)
, 63 C.C.C. (3d)
419, 5 C.R.R. (2d) 372, 71 Man. R. (2d) 49, and by one of its members in
R.
v.

Clemente
(1993),
1993 CanLII 4410 (MB CA)
, 86 C.C.C. (3d) 398, 27 C.R. (4th) 281, [1994] 2 W.W.R.
153.

Having regard to all of those authorities, both
old and new, I am not persuaded that any weight should be given to the
obiter

comments of this court in
R.
v.
Law

(1909),
1909 CanLII 302 (MB CA)
, 19 Man. R. 259,
or to the decision in
R.
v.
Georgia Straight Publishing Ltd., McLeod
and Cummings
,
1969 CanLII 834 (BC SC)
, [1970] 1 C.C.C. 94, 4 D.L.R. (3d) 383, 6 C.R.N.S. 150 (B.C.
Co. Ct.), to the effect that an intention to defame is not an element of
defamatory libel. I have no hesitation in holding that to convict a person of
publishing defamatory matter known to be false, the Crown must prove an
intention to defame.

That being the case, the unintended defamation
of another is not an offence, at least under s. 300. This removes from the
reach of the offence a person who believes, according to his or her own values,
that the words used are not defamatory — as, for example, a member of a fascist
organization stating that a person is anti-Semitic (the example is taken from
Working Paper No. 35 of the Law Reform Commission of Canada at p. 19). It also
removes from the offence's reach the newspaper person who feels constrained to
report the defamatory words of another, even if he or she knows them to be
untrue, if the sole intent in publishing them is to inform readers that the words
were said.

As an intent to defame is required, it follows
that the
mens rea
element of the offence is not vague.

That the offence covers trivial as well as
serious defamations

There is now strong authority for saying, at
least in England, that only a serious libel can be the subject of a successful
prosecution: see
Gleaves
v.
Deakin, supra,
in which Viscount Dilhorne,
with the concurrence of Lord Keith of Kinkel, said (at p. 487) that a criminal
libel must be a serious one, and Lord Scarman said (at p. 495) that it must be
a grave one. Viscount Dilhorne went as far as suggesting (at p. 486) that, if a
trial judge thought the libel trivial, he might direct the jury to acquit.

Eventually, when
Gleaves v. Deakin
was
tried (the House of Lords having heard the case on a preliminary issue only), Comyn
J. directed the jury that a criminal libel was "a written statement so
serious in itself, and so greatly affecting a person's character and
reputation, as to justify invoking criminal law and punishment instead of, or
as well as, the civil law and damages": The Times, February 25, 1981 (news
item).

Gleaves
v.
Deakin

was a case of ordinary libel. It was, therefore, unnecessary to make a
distinction between that offence and one of publishing a libel known to be
false. As I will suggest in a moment, it may well be the ingredients of the
latter offence make it always one that is serious.

The notion of "seriousness" as an
element of the offence was commented upon by the English Law Commission in its
Working Paper No. 84. It stated (at p. 100):

[T]he notion of seriousness, as it exists,
is not tied to any rule by reference to which it is to be applied: it is not
clear, for example, whether in assessing the seriousness of the libel the jury
should have regard to the defendant's motive or purpose in publishing the
libel, the position of the person defamed, the harm
likely to be caused, the likelihood of a breach of the peace, or whatever.
Moreover, there is circularity in a rule which says that conduct of a certain
kind is a criminal offence if the jury regard it as sufficiently serious to
call it criminal.

Although this criticism of the notion of
seriousness may be valid in the case of ordinary libel, I think it is not when
the offence is that of publishing a libel known to be false. That offence is
always serious. What makes it so is the libeller's intention to defame, coupled
with the use of facts known to be false.

Regardless, then, of whether what was said in
the House of Lords applies in Canada, the offence of publishing a libel that is
known to be false is not overbroad for encompassing trivialities. The offence
is by its nature a serious one and, as such, sufficiently defined without
express reference to seriousness.

My view is supported by history. There is no
evidence of prosecutions under s. 300 for trivial libels. No doubt, fictitious
examples might be conjured up, but they would be more theoreti­cal than
practical and the Supreme Court has warned us against using extravagant hypotheticals:
see
R. v. Goltz
(1991),
1991 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, 67 C.C.C. (3d) 481 at pp. 503-4, [1991] 3 S.C.R.
485, 8 C.R. (4th) 82,
per
Gonthier J.

Besides, there are safeguards. Unlike England,
where most defamatory libels were prosecuted privately, Canada has laws which
discourage this. Mr. Stevens' counsel refers to the fact that the offence may
only be prosecuted on indictment as a weakness which leads to overbreadth. I
call it a strength, as it ensures that no one can be prosecuted to conviction
without the intervention of a provincial Attorney-General or leave of a judge:
ss.
574(3)
and
577
(d) of the
Criminal Code
.
It is true that a private person
may lay an information and proceed through a preliminary inquiry, but such a
person can proceed no further without intervention or leave. And, as we know
from experience, private people simply do not go this route. They take the
route which will ensure that the case will be tried: they sue the culprit
civilly.

Furthermore, I believe it would be open to a
judge, if trying the case alone, to acquit on the ground of triviality or, if
there is a jury, to direct it to do so. Quite apart from what was said by the
House of Lords in
Gleaves
v.
Deakin, supra,
it is a venerable
maxim of the law that it does not concern itself with trifles
(de minimis
non carat lex).
And, if all this failed, it would still be open to a judge
to give the accused person an absolute discharge on account of triviality.

That the offence covers the expression
of
opinion

This, in my view, simply is not so. A defamatory
libel is defined as matter that is likely to injure a person's reputation. But,
for its publication to constitute an offence under s. 300, "it (is) the
duty of the prosecution to satisfy the jury that the alleged libel was not only
false, but that the appellant knew it to be false":
per
Avory J. delivering
the judgment of the English Court of Criminal Appeal in
R. v. Black,
The
Times, November 16, 1932. (This statement is to be preferred to that of du Parq
J. in
R. v. Wicks, supra,
to the effect that the accused must justify
his libel, as this latter statement was apparently made
per incuriam
and
is inconsistent with post-Charter law in Canada.)

Unlike a statement of fact, an opinion is
neither true nor false. It is simply the view of the person who holds it. It
would be impossible, then, for the Crown to prove either falsity or know­ledge
of falsity so as to discharge its burden.

It is true that fact and opinion are often
intertwined. It is difficult sometimes to draw a line between them. None the
less, it is done in civil actions all the time.

The situation is entirely unlike that considered
by McLachlin J. in
R. v. Zundel, supra,
at pp. 518 and 519, where there
was room for confusion between historical fact and opinion. That was a case in
which the accused was charged with spreading allegedly false news about the
Holocaust. As McLachlin J. pointed out, the spreading of news "encompasses
a broad range of historical and social speech, going well beyond what is patent
or provable to the senses as a matter of `pure fact' ". That is not so
when we are talking about a libel published with respect to a living person.

One of the great dangers of a crime encompassing
the spreading of false news is that what is false will be determined by
reference to what is generally accepted as true. This is so, at least in part,
because of the difficulty of proving historical facts. As McLachlin J. noted
(at p. 519):

The danger is not confined to totalitarian
states like the Nazi regime in Germany or certain communist regimes of the past
which blatantly rewrote history. We in Canada need look no further than the
"not so noble savage" portrayal of native Canadians in our children's
history text books in the early part of this century.

I cannot deny that, if a well-respected public
figure were defamed, there would be a danger of a jury accepting his or her
reputation as proof of the falsity of an assertion against it. But I do not see
the difficulty this presents as being either as serious as that in dealing with
historical facts, or insurmountable. In a case involving the defamation of a
living person, we are dealing with relatively current facts which can be proved
and judges can warn themselves or juries of the need for actual proof of
falsity as a pre­condition to a conviction.

Whatever difficulties exist in distinguishing fact
from opinion, and in proving falsity of fact, the alternative is to say that in
our post-Charter society there can be no criminal sanction for the character
assassin. Even if a new crime, defined in the terms proposed by the English Law
Commission, was created, those same difficulties would still exist. This
alternative I find to be discordant with the values of a free and democratic
society in which, to repeat what the Canadian Law Reform Commission said,
"deliberate character assassinations ought not to be tolerated".

That the offence is committed by mere insult

I doubt that this is so. It is true that
"defamatory libel" is defined to include matter that is
"designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is
published". This makes an insult sufficient for a conviction on a charge
of ordinary libel, but, if the insult is not also defamatory in its primary
sense, I do not understand how it can be sufficient for a conviction under s.
300. An insult need not be more than a scornful, insolent or disrespect­ful
remark. Unless otherwise defamatory, such a remark would be neither true nor
false. It would simply be rude. The Crown could not prove falsity.

In any event, the matter published in each of
the cases before us was clearly defamatory in its primary sense. It is,
therefore, unnecessary for us to decide whether an insult that is not otherwise
defamatory is sufficient for a conviction under s. 300 or, if it is, whether
that aspect of the crime is constitutional. The point should be left for
consideration when it actually arises.

That the offence is committed by publishing
the defamatory matter
to
the person defamed
alone

The defamatory matter published in each of the
cases before us was published to at least one third party. Following the
principle that we not decide more than required by the facts of the case before
us, I would leave to another day the question of whether the provision
criminalizing the publication of a known-to-be­untrue defamatory libel to the
person defamed alone is constitu­tional.

It is possible to do this because that manner of
publication is not an integral part of the offence and may, if necessary, be
severed. That, I think, would be the proper course rather than striking down
the entire offence for overbreadth.

That the offence encompasses defamation of a
corporation

The defamatory matter in each of the cases
before us was published of a living person. Following the same principle as
before, I would leave to another day the questions of whether the word
"person" in the definition section includes a corporation, and, if
so, whether the crime of publishing defamatory matter that is known to be false
about a corporation is constitutional.

Here again, there is no reason to strike down
the entire offence for overbreadth when publications about corporations can be
severed from the rest and dealt with separately. The alternative is to decide
an important issue in a factual vacuum.

That the offence will have a chilling effect
on legitimate publishers

In my Temple days, I had a barrister friend who
was engaged by a leading newspaper as a libel reader, scanning copy nightly for
potential defamations. Occasionally, he advised against publishing a statement
which was defamatory of an individual and might not be true, but most
frequently he simply ensured that the paper had reasonable grounds for making a
statement which spoke ill of someone. The dividing line was a supportable
belief in truth.

It so happened that my friend was not always
right. The paper was sued for libel, and it turned out that what it had
published about someone was not true. An apology had to be made and an offer of
amends. But never, as far as I am aware, was the paper prosecuted for
publishing matter which it knew to be false.

I really do not understand how anyone can be chilled
by a law which forbids the publication of facts about a person that are known
to be untrue. An innocent person might fear prosecution if the law in question
forbade the publication of false facts. That which is believed to be true may
in truth not be. But, when knowledge of falsity is the criterion of guilt, I
totally fail to understand how the publication of any information which is not
known as false can be said to be chilled.

I dare say that, in the imagination, one can
conjure up instances in which the reputation of a person is so good that any
adverse allegation against that person will be assumed false. But assump­tion
of falsity is not a proper basis for convicting the maker of the allegation of
the crime of publishing a false libel: it must be proved that he or she knew it
to be false and that defamation was intended. The crime is far too well
designed to chill the innocent!

Mr. Stevens' counsel offers a number of
illustrations of alleged libel chill. He points to the recent depiction, on the
cover page of a magazine, of a well-known, right-wing politician with a Hitler-style
moustache. I suppose some people might be chilled from making that depiction,
but the actual publisher of the cartoon was not! Nor was there reason for the
publisher to have been. As Seaton J.A. said in
Vander Zalm
v.
Times
Publishers
(1980),
1980 CanLII 389 (BC CA)
, 109 D.L.R. (3d) 531 at p. 539, 12 C.C.L.T. 81, [1980] 4
W.W.R. 259 (B.C.C.A.): "[C]artoons are (not) to be interpreted literally.
That is not how they are seen by ordinary persons or by the law."

A further illustration of alleged libel chill
was borrowed from the majority judgment in
R. v. Zundel, supra,
in which
reference was made to the chilling effect of the crime of spreading false news.
There, it was suggested that an environmental activist might be chilled from
saying that rain forests are being destroyed. Mr. Stevens' counsel urges us to
accept that that same activist might be chilled from saying: "Company A
and its friend (naming a leading politician) are destroying the rain forests."
What non- sense! Such a statement, in reference to a person, is clearly an
opinion. It is an interpretation of primary facts which may lead others to a
different conclusion.

Counsel also suggested that the satirist may be
chilled by the law embodied in s. 300.1 dare say that is so if the satirist
wishes to use known lies about a person in order to expose the person to
ridicule, but surely that is as it should be. Even in the guise of literature
or political comment, no one should have a right to tell deliberate lies about
another for the purpose of making the person appear ridiculous. The true
satirist achieves his or her proper goal by the skilful use of truth, or of
what is believed to be true, and usually does so by exposing vice in general
and not that of a particular individual. No example was given to us of
satirical comment which would unreasonably be chilled by this law.

In the same vein, counsel suggested that the
maker of the hyperbolic statement would be chilled. I do not think that that is
so as long as the point being made by the statement is not itself a known lie.
A statement that a man is a mass murderer, when he has only killed two or
three, does not involve a lie. Perhaps the term "mass" would be
excessive, but clearly not to the extent that the maker of the statement need
be chilled by s. 300. It would be different, of course, if the subject of the
hyperbolic statement had, to the knowledge of the maker, killed no one at all,
but that is as it should be.

Such was the genius of those who devised this
particular crime that they limited it to the publication of a fact which is not
only defamatory of a person, but is also false, known to be false and intended
as defamatory. Surely such a crime will chill no one from a proper exercise of
free expression.

Conclusion on overbreadth

Having considered all of the instances of
alleged overbreadth, I am driven to the conclusion that the crime passes the
minimal impairment test. In so concluding, I rely, of course, on the high value
to be given to the law's objective and the lack of worth in the expressive
activity of intentionally defaming someone by the publication of known lies.
Only a mechanistic approach, which we are not to use, could lead to the
opposite conclusion.

(3)
Balance

A law which passes the minimal impairment test
may still be struck down if its adverse effects on the
Charter
right or freedom
in question are so severe that they outweigh either the importance of the law's
objective or, where the objective is only partially achieved, its salutary
effects on the mischief to be cured: see
Dagenais
v.
Canadian
Broadcasting Corp. (S.C.C.,
judgment rendered December 8, 1994) [now
reported
1994 CanLII 39 (SCC)
, 94 C.C.C. (3d) 289, 120 D.L.R. (4th) 12, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 835].

In this particular case, as I have said repeatedly,
the adverse effects on free expression are minimal, inasmuch as the expressive
activity affected is of the lowest value. In contrast, the objective of the law
is of the utmost importance and, although not perfectly achieved, is
sufficiently so to make what is achieved more valuable than the expression
which the impugned law limits. It may be impossible to prove, but I cannot help
thinking that s. 300 of the
Code
contributes greatly to the relative
infrequency of deliberate libels published with knowledge of falsity. That
being so, imbal­ance is not an issue.

Result

In the result, I am of the view that s. 300 is
constitutional; that the conviction appeals from the verdicts of L. Giesbrecht Prov.
Ct. J. should be dismissed; that the appeal from the acquittal by Simonsen J.
should be allowed; and that in its place a conviction should be entered. The
appeal from the sentence imposed by L. Giesbrecht Prov. Ct. J. should be given
a hearing date and the other case remitted to Simonsen J. for sentencing. I
would so order.

We have reviewed those submissions and are in
